Shennong Bencao Jing
(The Classic of Materia Medica of Shennong)

Recorded by Wu Pu and others of the Wei dynasty
Compiled by Sun Xingyan and Feng Yi of the Qing dynasty

Preface to the Shennong Bencao Jing (Classic of the Divine Husbandman's Materia Medica)

The Record of Rites states: "One should not take medicines from a physician whose family has not practiced medicine for three generations." Zheng Kangcheng explained: "This means being careful about the preparation of medicinal compounds." Kong Chongyuan, citing an outside commentary, explains that "three generations" refers to: first, the Yellow Emperor's acupuncture and moxibustion; second, Shennong's materia medica; and third, the Plain Woman's treatise on pulse diagnosis. Kangcheng's Commentary on the Rites of Zhou also states that the five medicines are: herbs, wood, insects, minerals, and grains. The art of combining these into medicinal preparations belongs to the tradition of Shennong and Ziyi. Thus what the Commentary on the Rites of Zhou means by "being careful about compounds" refers specifically to the materia medica texts and their teachings. Kong Chongyuan, having accepted the theory of combination, then doubted its orthodox interpretation — this was going too far. The History of the Han Dynasty cites the Bencao Fangzhu as the first text to record the Shennong Bencao Jing in three volumes. Cai Yong's bibliography lists a materia medica in seven volumes, but both are now lost. The Bibliographic Treatise omits any record; Jia Gongyan's Zhongjing Bibliography lists a Bencao Jing attributed to Ziyi in one volume, without attributing it to Shennong. It was not until the Sui Dynasty's Bibliographic Treatise that the Shennong Bencao Jing in three volumes was recorded. According to citations in Lu Yuanlang's Jingdian Shiwen, the title is indeed the Shennong Bencao Jing in three volumes. The present division into upper, middle, and lower grades of medicinal substances corresponds with this, suggesting the text circulated in this form since the Han dynasty. The Sui bibliography also records Lei Gong's Bencao Jizhu in four volumes and Cai Yong's Bencao in seven volumes, but both are now lost. From the Bielu onward, there were successive additions and deletions, rises and reductions in classification, recorded as circumstances arose, or transmitted together with the original text without distinction. Sun Boyan borrowed his nephew's copy and, using the Daguan Bencao where texts are distinguished in black and white characters, determined that certain passages were later interpolations. The Taiping Yulan cites the classic most extensively from the oldest scattered sources found in various books; entries so cited were established as the original text. Place names such as Yuzhang, Zhukun, Changshan, and Fenggao counties were used as evidence — this was no arbitrary elegance. As for Wu Pu's version of the materia medica, it is the oldest text, and passages cited scattered in various books were established as the original text. Such an undertaking required deep and sustained thought — it was no easy task. All creatures — the great officers who breathe and bear vital energy, those born upside down, those who labor and wriggle, the gnats that fly and swarm — each has its nature fully realized in response to things, giving them life. The learned should give this careful thought. The Huainanzi states: "Rehmannia (dihuang) governs the bones, and licorice (gancao) governs the regeneration of flesh." It also states: "Euphorbia (daji) expels water retention, and woad seeds (tingli) relieve swelling; if used without proper measure, they will instead cause illness." The Lunheng states: "Wind ailments are treated with wind-related herbs; heat ailments are treated with heat-related herbs; borderland ailments are treated with honey and cinnabar." The Qianfu Lun states: "When treating illness, one must use genuine ginseng; conversely, if one obtains Zhiluo as a substitute, or Ophiopogon in place of something else, and the substitute is used without recognizing the genuine article, combining and taking them — the illness will only grow worse." This is the gist of Shennong's legacy.

Publisher's Note

The Shennong Bencao Jing (Classic of the Divine Farmer's Materia Medica) is China's oldest pharmaceutical document. Traditionally attributed to the Divine Farmer (Shennong), it was in fact composed by later hands under his name. According to successive generations of scholarly verification, it is likely a work from the late Eastern Han period, and took shape as a dedicated text through the compilation and commentary of Wu Pu of the Wei state. Later, more comprehensive materia medica works — such as the Tang dynasty's Bencao (revised by Su Jing and others), the Song dynasty's Jingshi Zhenglei Beiyong Bencao by Tang Shenwei, and the Ming dynasty's Bencao Gangmu by Li Shizhen — all took the Shennong Bencao Jing as their foundation and expanded upon it.

Wu Pu's compilation drew widely from sources such as the Yiwen Leiju, the Chuxue Ji, and commentary on the Hou Han Shu, among other works, and contains many citations. During the Jiaqing reign of the Qing dynasty, Sun Xingyan, drawing on the Taiping Yulan and the Zhenglei Bencao and other widely gathered sources, compiled a recension of the Bencao, appending one additional volume of textual variants. Each cited passage from various books was appended after its relevant entry, making this a relatively thorough standalone edition. Ming scholar Lu Fu extracted the Shennong Bencao Jing text from the Bencao Gangmu and compiled it separately. There was also a compilation included in the Wuling Shanren Yizhu Qi collection. The Bencao Jing was incorporated into the Hanxue Tang Congshu; and in the Qing, Zhou Hai published the Shennong Bencao Jing in three volumes with one appended volume of variants. This book makes selective corrections to individual characters and sentences. Sun's recension, though it still contains certain errors and omissions, is nonetheless relatively thorough and well-documented in its collation and commentary. This reprint uses the old printing blocks; textual problems identified during proofreading are explained in the appended "Note on Collation."

The Commercial Press
March 1955

Preface to the Shennong Bencao Jing (Divine Farmer's Classic of Materia Medica)

A Confucian scholar need not be famous as a physician in order to understand the principles of medicine — yet no one has surpassed the Confucians in this understanding. In the time of the Spring and Autumn period, those who were truly Confucians were the ones the world first praised as physicians, placing Shennong above all, not as one who wandered with the immortal Taiyi, but as one whose teachings were transmitted to physicians. He mastered the Zhou Yi and understood the significance of creatures and vessels. He was a physician in that sense. Without broad knowledge, without knowing the tens of thousands of plants, minerals, and creatures produced across the land — without testing and personally tasting them to determine whether they can heal — one's practice will lack spiritual depth and will not be properly transmitted. Even if one were to travel the Five Sacred Mountains and Four Great Rivers collecting jades, stones, herbs, trees, birds, beasts, insects, fish, grains, and cereals, and test them all, one would amount to no more than a merchant or market vendor. What would that have to do with medicine? I have considered that Shennong was one of the greatest Confucian scholars of all antiquity. The Chongwen Zongmu records works attributed to Shennong including a volume on food items and a volume on the five visceral organs. The Bencao Jing too has no single authoritative original text; from the Tang dynasty onward it was reviewed and compiled. The Daguanbencao, as the Zhulei Bencao notes, ceased to be widely transmitted for a long time, and those who followed — such as Xi Yong with his commentary and Lu Yi with his additions — all based themselves on the original classic, yet either incorporated hidden sayings or elaborated interpretations, so that meanings became ever more fragmented and obscure. No one had yet produced a refined, careful, and illuminating critical text, making it difficult to verify the ancient writing, and even more difficult to reach a balanced judgment. Sun Yuanru, through his connections as a commissioner and the work of his nephew Fengqing, compiled the Shennong Bencao Jing in three volumes, drawing on the Wushan, Erya, Guangya, Huainanzi, and Baopuzi and other texts, without listing ancient prescriptions — not merely to demonstrate the pulse tradition, but so that the intentions of the ancient sages, Shennong's healing of the world, would shine forth as clearly as one's eyebrows. Confucius said, "Broadly acquaint yourself with the names of birds, beasts, plants, and trees," and also, "The extension of knowledge lies in the investigation of things." Thus this book is entirely appropriate. Some have doubted the Bencao Jing because the name "bencao" (materia medica) first appears in the Han Shu under the record of Emperor Ping and in the biography of Lou Hu. Yet Shennong first tasted the hundred herbs and first established medicine and pharmacy, as seen in three volumes, which later editors appended by county and district. The original classic only says "grows in mountain valleys" or "grows in river marshes." The Hongfan...

The imperial annals record that because of the 365 types, sacrificial offerings were made, and further annotations were added, fixing the text of the Bencao; later compilers expanded it to twenty volumes, adding 114 types. Shennong first tasted the hundred herbs and established medicine; Tang dynasty scholars of the classic added 133 types; sacrificial editions were further annotated and fixed, and the Bencao was again compiled, with county and district information appended by later people. The classic itself only says "grows in mountain valleys" or "grows in river marshes." Hongfan...

Publication Preface

Preface to the Shennong Bencao Jing

Because those who delved deeply into this subject were broadly learned, they drew analogies and comparisons across categories, all in accord with pharmaceutical discourse. Later Confucians sometimes dismissed this as mere talk of technical arts and crafts, lumping it together with hunting and fishing lore. Moreover, those who had not studied under a master and who departed from antiquity went so far as to obscure the names of birds, beasts, grasses, and trees recorded in the canonical texts, passing errors along until the original meanings were lost. Already in the biography of Hua Tuo in the History of the Later Han, it is recorded that Wu Pu studied under Hua Tuo, followed Tuo's methods of treatment, and cured many patients, using the Five-Animal Exercises as a separate transmission. It is also recorded that Emperor Ming of Wei had Pu compile the exercises for birds and beasts. Pu conveyed the methods to various physicians; some doubted that his techniques had been transmitted separately with esoteric texts and unusual formulas. Yet when one examines Pu's commentary on the Bencao today, one sees that it draws upon the sayings of the Yellow Emperor, Shennong, Qibo, Lei Gong, Tong Jun, Yi He, and Bian Que, as well as later famous physicians, omitting nothing. That he was able to cure so many patients was due to the diligence of his scholarly inquiry and verification — not necessarily because he possessed some separate esoteric texts or unusual formulas. It is truly said that one who has not read the books of three generations of physicians should not administer medicines. The texts of the Yellow Emperor, Shennong, and Bian Que that circulate in common society have largely been tampered with by later hands. I have long wished that men of broad learning and wide knowledge would set them right. Now, as Master Sun Bochang has collated and established the text of the Bencao and brought this matter to light, readers who wish to go further in examining its careful scholarship and precise annotations should seek that out for themselves.

Written by Shao Jinhan of Yuyao

Preface to the Collated Shennong Bencao Jing (Classic of Materia Medica of Shennong)

The three-volume Shennong Bencao Jing has been transmitted in white-character editions. As seen in the Daguan Bencao, the preface to the Jiayou Supplementary Commentary states: what is called the Shennong Bencao Jing uses red characters, while the additions made by later physicians building on Shennong's original entries use black characters interspersed among the red. The preface to the Kaibao revised edition states: the old text, based on these three transmitted volumes, had the black-character Mingyi Bielu (Supplementary Records of Famous Physicians) edited and compiled together with it by Tao Hongjing up to the time of the Elder of Huayang (Tao Hongjing), who added supplementary entries and incorporated the Bielu alongside the original classic, mixing red and black in the writing. This was considered a clear and evident arrangement. Thus the Mingyi Bielu that has been transmitted in the world was compiled by Tao Hongjing, who interwove the Bielu with the original classic. The earlier texts attributed to Shennong, the Yellow Emperor, Qibo, Lei Gong, and Bian Que each existed as separate writings. Wu Pu saw them all, and that is why his account of the properties and indications of drugs varies among different schools. Later people compiled them into a single text, yet naturally the order of the Bencao remained undisturbed, so that the original classic's text was not confused with old explanations, nor was the original text mixed with such sources as the Hanshu Pingji (Annals of Emperor Ping) and the biography of Lou Hu. According to entries in the bibliographic treatise, there are still marginal notes and distinctions between red and black characters. Thus the text of the original classic is not confused with Wu Pu's writings, which are mentioned only briefly in the Hanshu.

The seven-volume Shennong Huangdi Shiyao (Shennong and Yellow Emperor's Drug-Eating [text]) is today referred to in some editions as Shijin (Food Prohibitions). Jia Gongyan's commentary on the Rites physician passage cites its text and correctly writes Shiyao (Drug-Eating). Song scholars, not examining this carefully, doubted that the Bencao was among the Seven Summaries.

The Zhongjing (Central Classic catalogue) cites a one-volume Ziyi Bencao Jing by Jia Gongyan, which is probably the same work. The Liang Qilu (Seven Records of the Liang dynasty) lists a three-volume Shennong Bencao; the discrepancy in the number of volumes is a matter of how texts were divided and combined in different periods.

The divergences in combining and dividing: the world's books were not yet written when Shennong and the Divine Farmer flourished, and knowledgeable people have therefore doubted the classic on this account. Huangfu Mi, for instance, said this work consists of four volumes compiled by Tao Hongjing; his statement about the varying volume count has already been addressed earlier. The bibliographic treatise's statement is well founded.

The characters not yet transmitted concerning medicinal properties and indications should be identified by reference to the various scholars. Eventually, in Tong, this work was recorded in the transmission. This text should be grouped with the Suwen (Plain Questions) and similar works.

Among works on military affairs, the Five Phases, and miscellaneous divination, the classic is counted as a book of the Three Sovereigns, with Shennong among them. The Shiji states that the First Emperor of Qin did not destroy books of medicine, pharmacology, and divination, and so this classic was fortunate to survive alongside those.

The Yijing and the Chunqiu with their commentaries are also preserved. Yan Zhitui's Jiaxun (Family Instructions) says that the Bencao was composed by Shennong, yet it contains the names of commanderies and counties such as Yuzhang, Zhuya, Zhaoguo, Changshan, Fenggao, Zhending, Linzi, and Fengyi.

All these drug entries with place-names were assigned by later people and are not part of the original text. Tao Hongjing also says that the commandery and county names of provenance are from the Later Han period, and he suspects they were added in the records of Zhang Ji (Zhongjing), Hua Tuo (Yuanhua), and others. According to collated commentaries, Zhang Heng [also touches on this matter].

Publication Note, Part One

Preface to the Shennong Bencao Jing (Divine Farmer's Classic of Materia Medica)

To regard health and peace as blessings, and to speak of longevity and a life of ten thousand years — why should one doubt that long-term use of medicines to lighten the body and extend life is merely the talk of later-age Daoist practitioners? In general, a scholar's devotion to learning is like that of a physician: one opens and unravels learning, and seeks out the writings of great Confucians renowned throughout the land, tracing the origins and veins of their thought; examining and reviewing their diagnoses; distinguishing the upright from the deviant, settling right from wrong, and discerning the line between warmth and cold, balance and heat in the consideration of remedies. Written at Guanhua Villa in Zhanyuan Garden, on the fifteenth day of the tenth lunar month of the year jiwei, the fourth year of the Jiaqing reign, by Zhang Jiong of Xuancheng, recorded with reverence.

Those who write such works are like treasures of golden paste and jade-green water, like phoenix eggs of broad learning, who grind cinnabar and sip ink, devoting each day to scholarship as their sole endeavor — reaching back through thousands of years to the age of Fu Xi as if it were but a single day. How could this be possible without a devotion that is both singular and long-sustained? I alone find it strange that within this compilation there is said to be no remedy for the ailment of book-obsession. How I wish one could rouse Shennong himself and put the question to him.

The upper volume of the Classic of Herbs notes in its commentary: the origins of the nature of medicines, discussions of the names and manifestations of diseases. The middle volume says: jade, stones, herbs, and trees in three grades. The lower volume says: insects, animals, fruits, vegetables, grains, and combinations in three grades. These names were altered by later physicians. I now follow the ancient ordering. Furthermore, the Emperors' World Annals and Tao Hongjing's preface refer to four volumes; Zhang Yuxii says that according to the old text it also had four volumes; Han Baosheng likewise says that the Shennong Bencao comprised upper, middle, and lower volumes plus a table of contents, making four volumes in all. If that is so, the discrepancy between three and four volumes arises from the presence of the table of contents. Works such as Ge Hong's Essentials of Nurturing Life and the Taiping Imperial览 that cite the Shennong Classic sometimes say "according to Taiyi zi" or "Taiyi zi says" — all of which are absent from the received Classic, or may have been in the table of contents and cut by later editors. As for the text of the Classic itself: where 釋 has been written for 燧, 創 for 瘀, 淡 for 痰, 注 for 蛙, 沙 for 砂, 免 for 菟, and so on — these all arose from errors in transmission. I have collated against ancient sources and corrected them; one should not be alarmed at departing from common usage. In analyzing the classification of substances and citing various texts, the foundations lie in the Mao Odes, the Erya, Shuowen, Fangyan, Guangya, and the various philosophers and miscellaneous writers; Feng Luan contributed greatly to the supplementation. Written by Sun Xingyuan of Yanghu.

Preface to the Collated and Established Shennong Bencao Jing

3

Preface to the Collated Shennong Bencao Jing (Classic of the Divine Farmer's Materia Medica)

The Taiping Yulan (Imperial览) cites the Bencao Jing entry on Taiyi Yuyuliang, whose alternate name is Shinao (Stone Brain), said to grow in mountain valleys. This reflects the original text, which contained no names of commanderies or counties — those were additions by later physicians. Today's Daguan edition places these names in black characters, or combines them into the text, noting "such-and-such mountain valley, such-and-such commandery, river or marsh." This is likely a copyist's error; the original text was not like this.

After the time of Zhang Zhongjing and Hua Tuo, Wu Pu composed a Bencao (Materia Medica) based on Shennong's, comprising 441 substances. The Sui Jingji Zhi (bibliographic treatise) records that Wu Pu studied under Hua Tuo. The Liang bibliographic records note that Wu Pu's Bencao ran to six scrolls; the Jiayou Bencao states that Wu Pu's book was already lost by his own time, and only scattered quotations survive. Today the full text no longer exists; it survives only through citations in compendia such as Chuxuji, Beitang Shuchao, annotations to the Hou Han Shu, Shilei Fu, and other works. The Taiping Yulan cites it most extensively. These sources supplement what is lacking in the Daguan edition. The present work therefore draws on Wu Pu's text and appends it to the main classic as a rough supplement. Where Wu Pu's explanations are cited, they derive from the main classic; the Daguan edition sometimes misrepresents these as black-character entries.

The total number of drugs appearing to exceed 365 is due to later persons arbitrarily splitting or combining entries; it is difficult to determine what is original. Some entries were clearly added by later hands, whether through oral transmission corrupting old names, or through other means.

Regarding the use of wine macerations: some argue that wine did not exist in Shennong's time. But the Bencao Yanyi has already addressed this by citing the Suwen. Similarly, attributing the text to the time of the Yellow Emperor need not be doubted from the outset. The Wenxuan commentary and the Bowu Zhi both record that Du Kang invented wine, and a letter ending a friendship with Du Kang mentions that at the time of the Yellow Emperor people could not yet obtain it from afar; one should not neglect to consult medical and pharmacological texts.

Scholars who slavishly follow vulgar editions without examining old versions, not checking for discrepancies in drug properties, have been misled. Li Shizhen of the Ming dynasty compiled the Bencao Gangmu; yet by his time names had become corrupted, and he merely took the Daguan edition, fragmenting the old text. He made arbitrary additions and emendations that have confused later students.

This present work was compiled together to complement and complete the classic and to enlighten those who study the arts of healing. The original preface by Tao Hongjing (written in red) states that the Upper Classic contains the upper-grade drugs, the Middle Classic the middle-grade drugs, and the Lower Classic the lower-grade drugs — the ancients divided the work into scrolls by category (minerals, plants, trees, etc., upper, middle, and lower grades), with a separate scroll for the general catalogue.

Shennong Bencao Jing (Divine Husbandman's Classic of Materia Medica), Volume One

Upper Canon

The upper-grade drugs, one hundred and twenty kinds, serve as sovereign medicines. They nourish life in accordance with Heaven, are non-toxic, and can be taken in large doses or over long periods without harming the person. Those who wish to lighten the body, augment the qi, resist aging, and prolong life should refer to this Upper Canon.

Compiled and transmitted by Wu Pu and others of the Wei dynasty.
Collated jointly by Sun Xingyan and Sun Fengyi of the Qing dynasty.

Upper Grade [Materia Medica]
Jade and Minerals Section

Cinnabar: flavor sweet, slightly cold. Governs the hundred diseases of the body and five viscera. Nourishes the spirit, calms the hun and po souls. Supplements qi, brightens the eyes, destroys malevolent spirits and demons. Long-term use opens communication with the divine and prevents aging; can be transformed into mercury. Found in mountain valleys.

Mica: flavor sweet, balanced. Governs dead skin on the body. [Treats] wind-cold and fever with sensations as if riding in a cart or boat. Eliminates pathogenic qi, stabilizes the five viscera, benefits the essence of children. Brightens the eyes; long-term use lightens the body and extends years. Found in mountain valleys.

[Note:] "Grows in mountain valleys" — this phrase is quoted in the Taiping Yulan. Later people have commonly added the three characters "mountain valley county ears," but these should be changed back to the original characters. All appear in black text; those below follow this convention.

Wu Pu's Bencao states: Cinnabar — Shennong says: sweet; Huangdi says: bitter, toxic; Bianque says: bitter; Master Li says: greatly cold. Grows in Wuling; can be collected at any time; when transformed, yields mercury and lodestone.

[Salty water section — Taiping御]

The Mingyi Records say: The true name is Zhenzhu (vermilion); it is bright in color like mica, can be split apart; the superior kind is born in the mountain valleys of Fuling, and can be collected at any time.

Investigation: The Shuowen says it is the red stone of Ba and Yue. The character depicts the mining of cinnabar wells, and the shape of cinnabar; the ancient form is also written as Tong. "Sha" (sand) means loose stone. Cinnabar transforms into mercury.

The Guanzi, chapter "Dishu," says: In the mountains of Ba there is cinnabar; beneath it is white gold (platinum). The Huainanzi, "Dixing" chapter, says: The red heaven, after seven hundred years, produces red cinnabar; after another seven hundred years it produces...

Gao You's commentary says: Red cinnabar is cinnabar. The Shanjing says: Dan (cinnabar) millet — "sha" is the relaxed pronunciation of the same sound. "Sha" was formerly written as "砂," but this is not mercury; i.e., it is an abbreviated character. The Liexian Zhuan says: Chi Fu [a Daoist adept]...

Bai-jiao (White Glue/Gelatin).

The chapter on Immortal Medicines states: Jade can be dissolved in crow-rice wine or di-yu wine to become water. It can also be dissolved with scallion juice to become powder, or sweetened into pills, or burned into powder. If taken for one year or more, one will not be wetted by water, not scorched by fire, not cut by blades, and no poison can harm. However, jade already fashioned into vessels should not be used — it benefits nothing and harms people. One must obtain unworked raw jade. The white jade from the kingdom of Khotan is the best; next is the jade from the border region of Xu-shan Pavilion in Nanyang; and also jade found in the waters of Lurong in Rinan — all are good.

Stalactite (Zhong Ru /钟乳石): flavor sweet, warm. It governs coughing with rising qi, brightens the eyes, benefits essence, calms the five viscera, opens the hundred joints, benefits the nine orifices, and promotes the flow of breast milk. The Imperial Encyclopaedia cites an alternate name: Gong Ru (Public Milk). The character "Gong Ru." Produced in mountain valleys.

Wu Pu states: Stalactite is also known as Xu Zhong (Hollow Center). According to Shennong: acrid. According to Tong Jun and the Yellow Emperor: harmonizing, sweet. According to Bian Que: sweet, non-toxic. The Imperial Encyclopaedia notes: greatly cold. Li [says]: produced in mountain valleys — the Imperial Encyclopaedia cites Taishan mountain valleys, in shaded places.

It forms from dripping juice along cliff faces. The juice gathers and drips; it looks like milk — yellow-white in color, hollow inside with connected passages. Collected in the second and third months, dried in the shade.

The Mingyi says: it is also called Gong Ru (Public Milk). The white kind is superior. Commentary notes: cited from the Imperially Reviewed Collectanea. Various texts such as the Lie Xian Zhuan state that pressing and consuming the stone marrow is called stalactite. Stalactite is described in the Han Shuo Wen.

Annex: Fan Zi Ji Ran states: stalactite is produced in Wudu. [Yellow...]

Increases years of life. Also named Yu Peng. Produced in mountain valleys. The Shan Hai Jing records this as "Zhong" with a substitute phonetic gloss; it is based on the local place-name graph. Stone Pu. Note. Flavor sour, cold. Governs cold and heat, diarrhea, white discharge, erosive sores, eye pain; strengthens sinews, bones, and teeth. Refined and taken as a food supplement, it lightens the body and prevents aging.

Lei Stone (泪石): mentioned in the Shan Hai Jing under the name "Xiang Stone." Stone cites: "the juice of milk-stone." The Shan Hai Jing Xiang commentary says: Yu Yan.

Wu Pu states: Yi Shi (藝石) is also called Yu Yan, also called Yu Ze. According to Shennong and Qi Bo: sour. According to Bian Que: salty. According to Lei Gong: sour, non-toxic. Produced in He Xi, or Long Xi, or Wudu. At Shi Men [cliff face], clusters [of it] without [end].

Qi Bo states: prolonged use harms the bones. The Imperial Encyclopaedia gives the alternate name Yu Yan. According to Shennong and Qi Bo: sour. Imperial Encyclopaedia.

The method of refining cinnabar at a mountain spring, taken together with talc as a mineral medicine — the ancients said that long-term use lightens the body and prolongs life, meaning one should give up grain and abstain from human intercourse, or take it for several decades before
the effects appear. When taken together with meat and food it tends to conflict and cause illness, so one should not doubt the truth of the ancient texts.

Mica (Yunmu): flavor sweet, balanced. Mainly treats dead skin on the body surface, wind-cold-heat [conditions], the feeling of being on a cart or boat, expels evil qi, calms the five viscera, benefits vital essence, brightens the eyes. Long-term use lightens the body and prolongs life. Also named Yunzhu, Yunhua, Yunying, Yunye, Yunsha, Linshi. Grows in mountain valleys.

According to medical records, it is found on Mt. Tai, Mt. Lushan in Qi, and among the rocks at Langya and Beiding mountains, and is gathered in the second month. Later records note that people combined them, so there is no way to distinguish them separately — these are the same as what is described in the writings of Zhang Zhongjing, Hua Tuo, and Pu's texts.

According to the Liexian Zhuan, Fang Hui refined and ate mica. Baopuzi's chapter on immortality medicines states: five-colored mica with predominantly blue-green is called Yunying and should be taken in spring; five-colored with predominantly red is called Yunzhu and should be taken in summer; five-colored with predominantly yellow is called Yunsha; five-colored with predominantly white is called Yunye and should be taken in autumn; five-colored with predominantly black is called Yunying and should be taken in winter. Pure crystal-white is called Linshi and may be taken throughout all four seasons.

What is called Yunmu — also named Yunjing — buried in the earth for ten thousand years will not decay. The Shuowen has no character for "lin"; the Yulan states lin means thin. This is another name for Yunmu.

Li Shan's commentary on the Wenxuan cites the Yiwu Zhi: soft mica is also named Yunpo (spirit of clouds); the Yulan also quotes: it lengthens muscle, benefits qi; long-term use enables tolerance of cold and heat, freedom from hunger and thirst, and immortality as a divine immortal.

Jade Spring (Yuquan): flavor sweet, balanced. Mainly treats the hundred diseases of the five viscera, softens sinews, strengthens bones, calms the hun and po spirits, lengthens muscle, benefits qi. Long-term use enables tolerance of cold and heat, freedom from hunger and thirst, and immortality as a divine immortal. Also named Yuzha.

If a dying person takes five jin of it, after death the body will not change color for three years. Also named Yumang. The Yulan notes: if one does not take it one will not attain long life; if taken early, one will not die.

Sun [Simo] says: taking it leads one to doubt — heaven and earth — not dying — growing in mountain valleys.

Shou Weng's body resembled white [jade]. Wu Pu says Yuquan is also named Yuxie; Shennong, Qibo, and Leigong rate it as sweet and balanced; Mr. Li rates it as balanced; it fears Donghua [winter flower], and dislikes green bamboo. Yulan: white Yumang resembles a white-headed duke, as the fu says in the same passage: it is entirely white and fine.

According to the Rites of Zhou, the Jade Steward section states that when the king fasts he is supplied with jade to eat. Zheng Xuan says jade is the pure essence of yang, and eating it wards off water qi. Zheng Siqing says that when the king fasts he should eat powdered jade. Baopuzi [also discusses this].

Wu Pu states: Tai Yi Yuyu Liang, also named Yu Ai. According to Shennong, Qibo, and Leigong it is sweet and balanced; according to Master Li it is slightly cold; according to Bianque it is sweet and non-toxic. It grows on Mt. Tai; it has a shell, and inside the shell there is white matter.

Long-term use lightens the body; one does not forget, does not become confused, or may extend one's years. Another name is Yao Jiu (Yao's leek). According to commentary, it grows on rocks above water and on stones. Those with nine nodes per inch are considered the best. Grows in pools and marshes.

The Mingyi (Celebrated Physicians) says: it is also called Shencao, also called Renwei, also called Tujing, also called Xueshen. Those shaped like a human form have spiritual power. Tianmendong (asparagus root): flavor bitter, balanced. It mainly treats all sudden wind-damp impediment conditions, strengthens the bone marrow, kills the three worms, removes hidden corpse pathogens. Note: no longer found growing wild in mountain valleys.

Chongwei Zi (Leonurus fruit): flavor acrid, slightly warm. Principal uses — brightening the eyes, replenishing vital essence, eliminating water qi. Long-term use lightens the body. The stem treats skin rashes and itching; can be used in a bath decoction. Alternate names: Penmu, Penming, Dazha.

Dodder [Tusizi]
The Immortal Medicines chapter says: Yu is also called Shan Ji and Shan Jing. The Sacred Medicine Classic says: if you truly wish to attain long life, take Shan Jing continuously.

Dodder seeds: flavor acrid, balanced [neutral]. Main [uses]: restores severed tendons and sinews, supplements insufficiency, replenishes qi and strength, fattens and invigorates. Wu Pu says: Dodder is also called Yu Nü [Jade Maiden], Song Luo, Niao Luo, Ya Luo, Fu Shi, and Chi Wang. [Imperial note/poetic reference]
The Mingyi says: it is also called Mian Si, Yu Wu, Tang Meng, Song Luo, Niao Luo, Ya Luo, Fu Shi, and Chi Wang. It grows in the fields of Chaozhou and in mountain valleys. Chi Wang is pale in color and large; the seeds ripen in the ninth month and are dried in the sun. [Poetic reference]
The Shuowen says: it is a creeping vine. The Guangya says: Mian Qiu means dodder. It is the female vine [nü luo]. The commentary says: Song Luo is pine-moss. Formerly written as Tu: flavor bitter, sour, acrid [imperial variant reading]. Ling [version] reads: [its] main [use is for] cold damage, cold injury [imperial/Ling variant]. Long-term use lightens the body and increases endurance.

The Bowuzhi (Record of Diverse Matters) states: The leaves of the yun-hao plant resemble those of the xie-hao herb. Maidong (Ophiopogon japonicus): Flavor sweet, nature balanced. Long-term use lightens the body, prevents aging, prevents hunger. It grows in river valleys and on embankments. One alternate name is yang-jiu (sheep leek). [Imperial览] citation says: Also called sui-zhi; the Taiyi name is pu-lei; also called ren-dong; also called bu-si-yao (medicine of immortality). [Various sources record] the alternate names: ma-jiu (horse leek), yu-jiu (Yu's leek), yu-yu-liang (Yu's surplus grain), yang-xu-jiu (sheep-beard leek), ren-ling, yang (sheep), ren-dong (winter-enduring), yu-liang (surplus grain).

Wu Pu states: One name is ma-jiu, one name is yu-jiu, one name is juan-dong, one name is yue, one name is ren-dong, one name is yang-xu-jiu.

Warm; according to Bian Que, non-toxic. It grows in fertile valley soil. Its leaves are like leek; it grows lush in moist ground in clumps. It fruits at no fixed season; the fruit is bluish-yellow. Also called yu-ge, also called yu-yu-liang; leaves like leek, evergreen through winter and summer, growing in valley grain fields.

The Mingyi states: In Qin it is called yang-jiu; in Qi it is called juan-jiu; in Chu it is called ma-jiu; in Yue it is called yang-xu. Another name is yu-yu-liang. The fruit is like green pearls; the roots resemble those of layered barley — hence the name mai-men-dong (barley gate winter).

Duhuo (Angelica pubescens): Flavor bitter, nature balanced. It governs injuries from wind-cold, metal-wound pain, ben-tun (surging-pig) syndrome, epileptic spasms, and women's shan-jia (hernial masses). Long-term use lightens the body and increases longevity. One name is qiang-huo, one name is qiang-qing, one name is hu-qiang.

The alternate name "Envoy" — it grows in river valleys.

Wu Pu states: Duhuo is also called hu-wang-shi-zhe (envoy of the barbarian king). According to Shennong and Huangdi it is bitter and non-toxic. It is gathered in the eighth month. This herb has flowers: when there is wind the flowers do not move; when there is no wind the plant sways on its own. [Imperial citation ends here]

Eminent physicians say: Also called Shanrong, Rucao Ye, and Yunhao — acrid and fragrant, edible. Grows in Hongnong and Yuanju. Roots are gathered in the second and eighth months and dried in the sun.

Prolonging life. One name is Mountain Yam (shanyù). It grows in mountain valleys.

Alisma (zéxiè). Flavor: sweet, cold. It governs: wind-cold damp impediment; difficult lactation; disperses water; nourishes the five viscera; augments qi and vital force; enriches and strengthens. Long-term use sharpens hearing and vision; prevents hunger; prolongs life; lightens the body; makes the face radiant; enables the body to move like water.

The Physicians' Record states: it is also called Hu Wang Shi Zhe (Envoy of the Barbarian King), and also called Du Yao Cao (Plant That Sways Alone). Examination: The Traditions of the Immortals records that Shan Tu took Qiang Huo and Du Huo; these two names both seem to refer to the same thing. "Hu Wang" and "Hu Qiang" all carry the character Qiang (meaning the Qiang people), just as "Zhuan Zhu" was also called "Zhuan She Zhu," and "Yu Gong Cha" was also called "Yu Gong." There is no other special significance to these names.

Che Qian Zi (Plantain seed): flavor sweet, cold, non-toxic. It governs urinary blockage, stops pain, promotes the flow of water passages and urination, eliminates dampness-impediment. Long-term use lightens the body, increases endurance against aging. Another name is Dang Dao.
The Imperial Survey notes: another name is Niu Yi (Cow's Trace), [marked in black characters].

It grows in flat marshy areas.

Guo Pu says it is what is now called Che Qian Cao (Plantain herb), with large leaves and long spikes, fond of growing beside roads; in Jiangdong it is called Ha Ma Yi (Toad's Coat), and also hides in cow dung. Qi Shi (shepherd's purse seed): flavor bitter, balanced. Primary actions: benefits the qi, fills out the muscles and skin, brightens the eyes, promotes mental acuity and foreknowledge. Long-term use prevents hunger and aging, lightens the body. Grows in mountain valleys.
Wu Pu: dry the fruit in the sun. (Kou's imperial note.)
Wu Pu says: Qi Shi, flavor bitter, sour, balanced, non-toxic; primary action is to benefit the qi, fill out the muscles and skin, brighten the eyes, promote mental acuity and foreknowledge; long-term use prevents hunger and aging, lightens the body; grows in Shaoshi mountain valleys; collected in the eighth or ninth…
month; dry the fruit in the sun.
The Famous Physicians say: grows in Shaoshi; collected in the eighth and ninth months; dry the fruit in the sun.
Commentary: Shuowen says qi belongs to the artemisia group; if it lives a thousand years it grows three hundred stalks; the Records of the Grand Historian, "Turtle Strategy" chapter, states that a qi plant of a hundred stalks shares one root.

The Mingyi records: grows on Zhongshan, harvested in the second month.

Examination: The Shuowen says "fan" means white wormwood (bai hao); "ai" means bing tai. The Guangya says fan-mu means lao-na. The Erya says ai means bing tai; Guo Pu says today's ai (mugwort) is bai hao. The Xia Xiao Zheng says the second month.

The Er'er zhuan says: fan comes from the hu, from hu means fan-mu, fan-mu means lao-bo. The Erya says fan-pang-hao; Guo Pu says bai hao, also fan from hu, Guo Pu says uncertain.

The Maoshi says: "to gather fan," the commentary says pang-hao. Also "fan-qi-qi," the commentary says fan is bai hao. Lu Ji says all ai of white color is pang-hao. The Chuci commentary by Wang Yi says ai is bai hao. According to this, pang and ai are similar in sound and meaning; ai is named in the Bencao Jing; those without it are bai hao. The Mingyi lists ai separately, which is not correct.

Chi Jian (Gastrodia elata): flavor pungent, warm. Main uses: kills ghost essences and malevolent things, eliminates gu-poison and evil qi. Long-term use increases qi and strength, nourishes yin, fattens and strengthens the body, and increases longevity. Also named Li Mu; also named Gui Du You. Grows in valleys.

Wu Pu says: grows in Chencang, Yongzhou, and Taishan Shaoshi; roots are harvested in the third, fourth, and eighth months and sun-dried.

Yuzhi (imperial encyclopedia): dried, treats swelling.

The Mingyi says: grows in Chencang, Yongzhou, and Taishan Shaoshi; roots harvested in the third, fourth, and eighth months. Sun-dry daily.

Also named Du Yao, also named Li Mu. The reason it is called He Li Mu: a separate account says the tian ma used by physicians today is this chi jian root, which has twelve lateral tubers encircling it, extending several chi from the main tuber.

The Baopuzi says: the immortal formulas include a plant called He Li Cao.

Although the parts depend on each other, they are not actually connected, but are linked through their qi. A separate account says: when this plant forms its underground root like a taro corm — that is this chi jian root — it has twelve lateral tubers circling it, several chi from the main tuber.

Yan Lü zi: noted also as yan na, yu lü.

[Formula for] not aging, growing in valleys.

Wu Pu says: Yan Lü — Shennong, Leigong, Tongjun, and Qibo all say it is bitter, slightly warm, non-toxic; Li's [classification] says warm. Or grows in Shangdang. The leaves are blue-green and thick, matched in pairs. Flowers are white in the seventh month; fruit is black in the ninth month.

Wu Pu says: Juanbai (Selaginella): Shennong classifies it as acrid; Tongjun and Leigong classify it as sweet. The Yulan encyclopedia cites: one name is Shenzhi; also called Shangugo. One name is [from another source].
The Mingyi (Noted Physicians) says: One name is Baozu (leopard foot); one name is Qiugu; one name is Jiaoshi. It grows on Changshan. Collected in the fifth and seventh months; dried in the shade.

Lanshi (Isatis/indigo fruit): Fan Zijiran says: Juanbai comes from Sanfu. One name is Biedu.
The Mingyi says: Its stems and leaves can be used to dye blue-green. It kills ghost-toxins from mosquito bites. Long-term use keeps the hair from turning white and lightens the body. It grows in flat marshes.
Commentary: Shuowen says "jue" is horse-indigo; indigo is a blue-dyeing herb. Erya says jue is horse-indigo. Guo Pu says: today this is the large-leafed winter indigo. The Rites of Zhou mentions dyeing herbs; Zheng notes that the dyeing herb is indigo. The Xiazhengzheng (Summer Ordinances) says: in the fifth month, the indigo begins to pour forth. The Book of Odes says "gathering indigo all morning long"; the commentary says indigo is a dyeing herb.

Commentary: Shuowen says: Shennong, the Yellow Emperor, Qibo, and Leigong classify it as acrid and non-toxic; Bianque classifies it as sour and non-toxic; Master Li says it is warm when fresh, cold when processed, or it grows on the shady side of Hutao Mountain.
Or [it grows on] Taishan ridge. The Yulan encyclopedia, or alternatively the Xiangguo source, says: leaves are fragrant, fine, blue-black in pattern, reddish like the drug-base plant; it grows in clumps through winter and summer; it flowers red in the fifth month; fruit turns black in the seventh month; two leaves at the tip of the hao stalk; collected in the third month.

The Mingyi says: One name is Xiangguo. Its leaves are named Yaomai. It grows in Wugong, in the Xiegu valley west of the ridge. Root is collected in the third and fourth months and dried in the sun.
Shuowen says: One name is Huhao; it is a fragrant herb. Sima Xiangru [mentions it in his rhapsody]. The Zuo Zhuan (Spring and Autumn Annals commentary) says: "there is mountain juhao." Du Yu says juhao is used to resist dampness to the west.
Yaoshuo says: It is also called Shanying or Yingxiang herb. Sima Xiangru's account, or written with the "bow" radical.
The Classic of Mountains and Seas says: Xiong (Ligusticum) – this plant is found in abundance as xiong-hao. Guo Pu says: Xionghao, one name is Jiangli. Fan Zijiran says xionghao grows without ever drying up; its quality is good. [Cited in] Sima Xiangru's rhapsody.
There is xionghao: Sima Zhen cites Sima Peng saying xionghao resembles the drug-base plant. Guo Pu says: today in Liyang it is called Jiangli.

Red Zhi (Ganoderma): flavor bitter, nature balanced. Governs chest constriction. Benefits heart qi. Supplements the center. Increases wisdom and intelligence. Prevents forgetfulness. Long-term consumption lightens the body, prevents aging, and extends life to the level of an immortal. Also called Dan Zhi.

Black Zhi: flavor salty, nature balanced. Governs abscesses. Benefits the water passages. Supplements kidney qi. Opens the nine orifices. Sharpens hearing and vision. Long-term consumption lightens the body, prevents aging, and extends life to the level of an immortal. Also called Yuan Zhi.

Green Zhi: flavor sour, nature balanced. Governs vision. Supplements liver qi. Calms the ethereal soul. Promotes benevolence and forbearance. Long-term consumption lightens the body, prevents aging, and extends life to the level of an immortal. Also called Long Zhi.

White Zhi: flavor acrid, nature balanced. Governs coughing and counterflow of qi. Benefits lung qi. Opens and benefits the mouth and nose. Strengthens the will. Promotes courage and fortitude. Settles the corporeal soul. Long-term consumption lightens the body, prevents aging, and extends life to the level of an immortal. Also called Yu Zhi.

Yellow Zhi: flavor sweet, nature balanced. Governs the five evils of the heart and abdomen. Benefits spleen qi. Calms the spirit. Fosters loyalty, trustworthiness, and contentment. Long-term consumption lightens the body, prevents aging, and extends life. Also called Mu Zhi.

Purple Zhi: flavor sweet, nature warm. Governs deafness. Benefits the joints. Protects the spirit. Supplements essential qi. Strengthens sinews and bones. Improves complexion. Long-term consumption lightens the body, prevents aging, and extends life to the level of an immortal. Also called Mu Zhi. [Note: the six types are also called Jin Zhi.]

Wu Pu says: Purple Zhi is also called Mu Zhi.

The Mingyi says: Red Zhi grows on Huo Mountain; Black Zhi grows on Heng Mountain; Green Zhi grows on Tai Mountain; White Zhi grows on Hua Mountain; Yellow Zhi grows on Song Mountain; Purple Zhi grows on high summer ground, is purple in color, and shaped like...

The Sanguan Yuji notes: all six Zhi are non-toxic. They are harvested in the sixth and eighth months.

The Chuci says: "Gather the triple-flowering herb on the mountain clearing." Wang Yi explains: "The triple-flowering herb refers to the Zhi plant." Guo Pu says the Zhi flowers three times in one year. The Liji, Nei Ze chapter, mentions Zhi. The Hou Han Shu, biography of Hua Tuo, mentions a lacquer-leaf and green-sticky powder. The commentary cites Tuo's biography: Zhi is a woody plant, also called Mei. Lu Zhi's commentary says the green-sticky variety is also called Di Jie.

One type called Yellow Zhi governs and regulates the five viscera and supplements essential qi. The character "jun" (mushroom) does not appear in older character dictionaries. It is traditionally said that Jin Nu Lian, as listed in the Liexian Zhuan, states that Lü Shang consumed Ze Zhi. The Bao Pu Zi, Xianyao chapter, states:

The red ones resemble coral; the white ones resemble cut fat; the black ones resemble the lacquer plant; the green ones resemble kingfisher feathers; the yellow ones resemble purple gold — all are luminous and translucent like solid ice. Also called Wan Sui (Ten-thousand Years). Grows in mountain valleys.

Juanbai (Selaginella): flavor acrid, nature warm. Grows in mountain valleys. Governs evil qi of the five viscera. Treats cold-heat pain in women's genitalia. Treats abdominal masses, blood obstruction, and inability to conceive. Long-term consumption lightens the body and improves complexion. Also called Wan Sui. Grows in mountain valleys.

Collected in the first month of the new year.

A note from the Classic of Mountains and Seas (Shan Hai Jing) states: "The mountain of Shang Shen is rich in resonant stones," suggesting this is the same substance. Guo Pu's commentary says: "Qing stone, a large rock, not quite right." The Tang dynasty commentary notes: "Its popular name is Nai Dong; people in the south of the mountains call it thus."

Ji Li Zi (Tribulus terrestris fruit): Flavor bitter, warm. Governs malign blood, breaking up concretions and accumulations, throat obstruction, and difficulty with lactation. Long-term use strengthens the muscles, brightens the eyes, and lightens the body. Also called Pang Tong, Qu Ren, Zhi Xing.

Luo Shi (Trachelospermum jasminoides): Named because it wraps around rocks and trees to grow. The Bie Lu calls it Shi Long Teng. Those growing on rocks are best.

Also named Ji Li, and Ci. Grows in flat marshes or roadsides. Harvest the fruit in the seventh and eighth months and dry in the sun.

A physician's note: "Also named Ji Ci, and Ci, grows at Feng Shuo; fruit collected in the seventh and eighth months and dried in the sun." [No text in the Jun version or Da Guan edition.]

A note from Shuo Wen says: Shou means Ji Li. The Book of Odes says: "The wall has Ci." Using Ci to mean Mao Man is incorrect. The Er Ya says: Ci is Ji Li. Guo Pu says: spreads along the ground, with fine leaves, the fruit has three corners and pricks people. Mao Shi says: the wall has inflammation, the commentary says inflammation means Ji Li. Old texts writing it as Ji Li are incorrect.

Huang Qi (Astragalus): Flavor sweet, slightly warm. Governs abscesses and festering sores, chronic wounds, draining pus, stopping pain, severe wind and leprosy conditions, five types of hemorrhoids, and rat fistulas. Supplements deficiency and treats all children's diseases. Also named Dai San. Grows in mountain valleys.

A physician's note: Also named Dai Shen, Du Shen, Shu Zhi, Bai Ben. Grows in Shu Commandery, Bai Shui, and Han Zhong. Collected in the second and tenth months and dried in shade.

Rou Cong Rong (Cistanche deserticola): Flavor sweet, slightly warm. Governs the five strains and seven injuries, supplements the middle, eliminates cold and heat pain in the stem, nourishes the five viscera, strengthens yin and benefits essence and qi, increases fertility, and treats women's concretions and accumulations. Long-term use lightens the body. Grows in mountain valleys.

A physician's note: Also written Rou Sui Rong or Rou Song Rong. According to Shennong and the Yellow Emperor it is salty; according to Lei Gong it is acidic and slightly warm; Li says it grows in Hexi and He Dong regions. Yu Kuan notes it grows in Shanyin, three to four inches long, in clumps. Also found in Dai Commandery and Yanmen. Collected from the second to eighth month and dried in shade.

Wu Pu says: Rou Sui Rong, also called Rou Song Rong. Shennong and Yellow Emperor say salty; Lei Gong says acidic and slightly warm; Li says grows in Hexi and Dai Commandery, Yanmen region. Collected second through eighth month, dried in shade.

A physician's note: Grows in Hexi and Dai Commandery, Yanmen. Collected on the fifth day and dried in shade.

Lan Jiao: flavor pungent, warm. It governs cough and counterflow, calms fright qi, repels evil and malignant influences, eliminates gu toxin and ghost-infixation, expels the three worms. Long-term consumption opens spiritual awareness. Another name: Wei Jiao. Grows in river marshes and pools.

Wu Pu says: also called Yuan Qiao; also called Xiong Qiong seedling. Grows in Yong Prefecture and Yuanju; collect leaves in the fourth and fifth months and dry in the sun.

Luo Shi (Trachelospermum): flavor bitter, warm. It governs wind-heat, dead flesh, abscesses and wounds, dry mouth, scorched tongue, swelling and abscesses that will not disperse, swelling of the throat and tongue, inability to swallow liquid. Long-term consumption lightens the body, brightens the eyes, moistens and nourishes the complexion, prevents aging, and prolongs years. Another name: Shi Ling. Grows in mountain valleys.

Wu Pu says: Luo Shi — also called Lin Shi, Ming Shi, Xian Shi, Yun Hua, Yun Ying, Yun Dan. Shennong [classifies it as] bitter, slightly warm; Leigong [classifies it as] non-toxic; Pian Que and Tong Jun [classify it as] sweet, non-toxic; Master Li [says] greatly cold. According to pharmacists, it is a sovereign herb; collect at any time. [Imperial citation note]

The Mingyi says: Another name is Su; it grows in the South Sea.

Xuduan (Dipsacus): flavor bitter, slightly warm. Main uses: treating cold-damage disorders; supplementing deficiency; gold-wound (sword-wound) abscesses and injuries; fractures and falls; knitting sinews and bone; difficulties in childbirth and in nursing. Long-term use increases vital energy.

Also called Longdou, also called Shuzhe; grows in mountain valleys.

The Mingyi says: Also called Jiegu (bone-joiner), also called Nancao, also called Huai. It grows on Changshan. Harvest in the seventh and eighth months; dry in the shade.

According to the Guangya: also called Bao Duan. The Fanzi Jiran says Xuduan comes from Sanfu. The Tongjun Yaolu says Xuduan grows as a trailing vine; the leaves are fine and trailing like perilla; the root is large, yellowish-white inside, and contains juice. Harvest the root in the seventh and eighth months.

Loulu: flavor bitter and salty, cold. Main uses: malignant sores; heat-type scrofula; goiter; scrofulous lumps; promotes milk secretion. Long-term use lightens the body, increases vital energy, sharpens hearing and eyesight, prevents aging, and extends years. Also called Yelan (wild orchid); grows in mountain valleys.

The Mingyi says: [text notes names and origins]

According to the Guangya: also called Feilian and Pianlu. Harvest the root in the eighth month; dry in the shade. Tao Hongjing says that in common usage the root is taken and called Luli.

Rong Shi (Rosa fruit): flavor sour, warm. Main uses: abscesses and malignant sores; hardening of flesh from injuries; dissipating pathological heat; erosion of the yin parts that will not heal. Wu Pu says: Also called Qiangwei, also called Niule, also called Qiangmi, also called Shanjie. Grows in Lingling and Shujun. Harvest in the eighth and ninth months; dry in the shade.

Puhuang [Typha pollen]: flavor sweet, balanced. It mainly treats pain in the abdomen beside the bladder, cold and heat, promotes urination, stops bleeding, disperses stagnant blood. Long-term consumption lightens the body, augments energy, prolongs life to that of an immortal. Grows in ponds and marshes.

According to the Pian Yu [dictionary]: the term "gao" refers to what is now the head of the cattail plant, which has a platform, and above the platform there is a double platform, from which the yellow [pollen] emerges — this is Puhuang. Xiangpu [Typha orientalis, fragrant cattail]: flavor sweet, balanced. Qian Gen (Madder root, Rubia cordifolia): flavor bitter, cold; governs cold-damp wind impediment, jaundice; supplements the center; grows in mountain valleys and streams.
The Mingyi (Famous Physicians) says: it can be used to dye crimson; another name is Di Xue (earth blood); another name is Ru Lu; another name is Mao Sou; another name is Qian. Grows on Qiao Mountain. The root is gathered in the second and third months and dried in the sun.

Xu Guang's notes to the Shiji say: Qian is also called Hong Lan; its flowers dye crimson-red-yellow. The entry for Hong Lan in the Mingyi is a separate herb, not the same thing.

Fei Lian (Carlina/Carline thistle, Carduus): flavor bitter, balanced; governs heat and swelling in the joints, sour pain; long-term use makes the body light. Grows in river marshes.
The Mingyi says: another name is Fu Tu; another name is Fei Zhi; another name is Mu He. Grows in Henei. Root gathered in the first month; flower gathered in the seventh and eighth months, dried in the shade. Grows in river marshes.

The Mingyi says: another name is Hui Ji; another name is Yuan Ji. Grows in the mountains of Qi and in Daijun. Gathered in the eighth month; dried in the shade.
Commentary: The Guangya says Hui Ji is Wu Wei Zi. The vine grows with berries clustered at the tips of the branches. The Baopuzi, chapter on immortal drugs, records five flavors.

Xuan Hua (Field bindweed, Calystegia): flavor sweet, warm; governs replenishing qi, removing facial dark spots [darkened complexion]. Makes the person's face beautiful and lustrous. Grows in rivers and marshes.

Physicians say: Also named Tianmen Jing, also named Yumen Jing, also named Zhilu, also named Chongge Lan, also named Guansheng. Found on level plains. Harvested in the fifth month.

Juemingzi [Cassia seed]: Flavor salty, neutral. Governs blindness, eye infections, skin redness, white films on the eye, red and painful eyes with tearing. Long-term use benefits the essence-light [vision]. [Reference to Taiping御 and other editions]. Lightens the body. Grows in rivers and marshes.

Wu Pu says: Juemingzi, also named Caojueming, also named Yangming [per the Yulanjuan].

Danshen [Salvia miltiorrhiza]:
Flavor bitter, slightly cold. Governs evil qi in the heart and abdomen, intestinal rumbling like rushing water, cold and heat, accumulations, breaks up conglomerations and removes masses, stops vexation and fullness, benefits qi. Also named Qichan Cao. Grows in valleys.

Grows at Tongbai or on Taishan mountain ridges, shaded slopes, small fragrant flowers, red roots, purple flowers in the fourth month, roots harvested in the fifth month, sun-dried.

Physicians say: Also named Chishen, also named Muyangru, also named Qichan Cao. Shennong, Tongjun, Huangdi, Leigong, and Bianque [all say] bitter, non-toxic. Li's [text says] greatly cold; Qibo [says] restrained.

Kochia scoparia (Di Fu Zi): Flavor bitter, cold. Governs bladder heat, promotes urination, supplements the center, and benefits essential qi. According to the Guangya: also called Di Mai; grows in Jingzhou; the fruit is gathered in the eighth and tenth months and dried in the shade. The Guangya says: flavor bitter and balanced; governs great heat, fire sores, bodily fever, vexation, evil and perverse qi; governs women's flooding and spotting with red and white discharge; lightens the body and brightens the eyes. One name Jie Huo; one name Shen Huo. The imperial commentary cites: also called Shui Yun.
[Note on Jing commentary]: grows in river valleys.
The Mingyi says: one name Huo Mu; one name Shu Huo; one name Liao Huo; grows on Mount Tai; gathered on the fourth day of the fourth month and the seventh day of the seventh month; dried in the shade.

It does not die over winter; it grows from the old stalks, hence the name Yin Chen Hao; the character Hao was added later. From this we know the old name was written as Yin Chen without Hao. Also, by the Guangya, Ma Xian is probably the same as Ma Xin Hao.
It belongs to the category of white artemisia.

Wu Pu says: Huaimu — according to Shennong and Leigong, it is non-toxic; grows in Jinping, Yanghe, and Hedong in level marshes; treats chronic cough, counterflow qi, internal injury, emaciation and deficiency; supplements the center and augments qi. [Imperial notation]

The Mingyi (Renowned Physicians) Record says: also named Tanmu; grows on Taishan; harvested at no fixed season.

According to Li Dangzhi: this is the camphor tree (zhang shu), a parasitic tree growing on it; large branches embed in the flesh. People today all use walnut bark as a substitute, which is wrong. The above are 73 herbs of the Upper Grade among the Grasses; formerly listed as 72 — examination shows the Six Zhi (mushrooms) should count as one, rising into the Shade category (yin). Both Huaimu and all grasses above should be entered here.

Mugui (male cinnamon): flavor pungent, warm; governs counterflow qi and cough, binding qi, throat obstruction, difficult breathing, benefits the joints, supplements the center and augments qi; long-term use penetrates the spirit, lightens the body, and prevents aging; grows in mountain valleys.

The Mingyi Record says: grows in Nanhai.

According to the Shuowen: "Gui is a tree of the Jiangnan region, the chief of all medicines." The Nanshan Jing says: "Mount Zhaoyao has much gui." Guo Pu says: "Gui leaves resemble loquat leaves, over two feet long and several cun wide; people today call thick-barked specimens Mugui or simply Gui — this is that plant." It has white flowers growing in clusters on mountain peaks, evergreen in winter and summer, with no mixed trees nearby. The Erya says: "Yuan is Mugui."

Gui (cinnamon): flavor pungent, warm; governs the hundred diseases, nourishes essence and spirit, harmonizes complexion, acts as a herald leading all medicines, promotes circulation; long-term use lightens the body, prevents aging, makes the face glow with radiance and beauty, keeping one like a child; grows in mountain valleys.

Jungui (tube cinnamon): flavor pungent, warm; governs the hundred diseases, nourishes essence and spirit, harmonizes complexion, acts as a herald leading all medicines, promotes circulation; long-term use lightens the body, prevents aging, makes the face glow with radiance and beauty, keeping one like a child; grows in mountain valleys.

According to the Chuci: "Mixed with Shenjiao pepper and Jungui cinnamon" — Wang Yi comments: Rong and Gui are both fragrant trees. The Liexian Zhuan says: Fan Li loved taking cinnamon.

Dang Ling: Guo Pu says that what is now called ci yu (thorny elm) is what the Ode "East Gate" calls fen, and the commentary explains that fen is the white elm. Lu Ji says its thorns are like those of the zhe tree, its leaves resemble elm, and when boiled as a vegetable it is smooth and pleasant like white elm. Sour Jujube (Ziziphus spinosa): flavor sour, nature balanced. It governs cold and heat in the chest and abdomen, pathogenic binding of qi, accumulation in the four limbs, aching and soreness, and damp bi-obstruction. Commentary from the Shuowen: "In Hedong it is harvested in the eighth month, dried in the shade for forty days." The Mingyi says it grows in Hanzhong and Yongchang.

Wall-wood (Bi mu): flavor bitter, nature cold. It governs heat binding in the five viscera and intestines and stomach, jaundice, intestinal hemorrhoids; it stops diarrhea, and women's flooding downward with red or white discharge, and erosive sores of the yin parts. Another name: tan huan. Grows in mountain valleys. Commentary: the Shuowen says棘 is the sour jujube. The Erya says棘 is the small jujube, which is what is called sour jujube. Dried Lacquer (Gan qi): flavor acrid, warm, non-toxic. It governs severed injuries, tonifies the center, reconnects sinews and bones, fills marrow and brain, calms the five viscera, addresses the five slackenings and six urgencies, and wind-cold-damp bi-obstruction. Fresh lacquer eliminates long worms. Taken long-term it lightens the body and resists aging. Commentary from the Shuowen: the zao and ji belong to the same category. The Mingyi says it grows in Hanzhong. It grows in river valleys. Commentary from the Shuowen: jie is a wood used to make arrows. The Shuowen says: the juice of the tai tree can be used to coat objects; its character is pictographic, showing the juice dripping down; the character for lacquer uses this as the water signifier. The Rites of Zhou, chapter on the Land Overseer, mentions the tax on lacquer groves; Yuan (Zheng Zhong) says the older text reads thus.

Cypress Seed (Bai Shi): Flavor sweet, nature balanced. Governs fright palpitations; calms the five viscera; supplements qi; eliminates dampness-impediment. [Commentary]: It resembles the appearance of firewood. One name is "Tuolu" — that is this herb. Also called "Immortal's Staff," or "Queen Mother of the West's Staff," or "Heavenly Gate Essence," or "Repel-Old," or "Earth Bone," or "Wolfberry."
The Shuowen says: bai is the quail. The Guangya says: "kuo-bai." The Bai leaves are especially good; harvest at all four seasons according to the cardinal directions, dry in shade. The Liji refers to xu. Fan Zi Jiran says cypress resin comes from the Three Adjuncts (Sanfu) region.
The Mingyi says: grows on Mount Tai; the cypress leaves are especially good; harvest at all four seasons according to the cardinal directions, dry in shade.

Poria (Fu Ling): Flavor sweet, nature balanced. Governs counterflow qi in the chest and flanks; anxiety, fright, and malign influences; fearful palpitations; binding pain below the heart; alternating cold and heat; vexation and fullness; coughing with counterflow; parched mouth and dry tongue; promotes urination. Long-term use calms the ethereal soul, nourishes the spirit, eliminates hunger, and prolongs years. Another name is "Fu Tu."
Wu Pu says: Poria calms the spirit. Tong Jun says: sweet, non-toxic; or grows at Mao Prefecture, from under large pine roots going three zhang one chi into the ground; harvested on the seventh day of the second month.

The Shiji (Chu Sheng commentary) and the Huainanzi Shulin Xun say: poria forms where dodder withers and dies; what was called "Fu Ling" lies beneath the dodder, shaped like a flying bird; "Fu Ling" is a thousand-year-old pine root; eating it prevents death.

Elm Bark (Yu Pi): Flavor sweet, nature balanced. Governs obstruction of urination and defecation; promotes water pathways; eliminates evil qi. Long-term use lightens the body and eliminates hunger. Its fruit is especially good. Another name is "Zero Elm." Grows in mountain valleys.
The Mingyi says: grows in Yingchuan; bark harvested in the third month, the white part taken and sun-dried; fruit harvested in the eighth month.
The Shuowen says: "yu" refers to the white-powder elm. The Guangya says: kuo elm and geng elm. The Erya says: elm, white-powder. Guo Pu says: the powder elm first grows leaves, then bears pods; the bark is white in color; also…

Magnolia bark: flavor bitter, cold. Governs great heat in the body when it is in the skin; removes facial heat, red pimples, rosacea from wine, malign wind, epilepsy, itching below the genitals, and clears the ears and eyes. One name: Lin Lan. Grows in river valleys.

Shennong Bencao Jing, Volume 1

It stays green throughout summer and has never been known to wither and fall; it appears to have joints and sections, hence its name. Chen Cangqi says it is the winter-green. The loquat tree resembles the kào [a type of oak]; used for vessels. The Shuowen says zhēn is a kind of tree; the Eastern Mountain Classic says that Mount Tai has many zhēn trees; Guo Pu says it is the female zhēn, whose leaves do not fall in winter; the Mao Odes say the southern mountains have Qi; Lu Ji says it is a tree. One name: Dog Bone — the grain is white and smooth; its seeds are like wooden fleas and can be combined into medicine. Sima Xiangru's rhapsody mentions the female zhēn; Gu says the female zhēn tree in winter [continues similarly].

Female Zhēn fruit: flavor bitter, balanced. Grows in Wuling; gather abundantly.
The Mingyi ji says: grows in Wuling; gather abundantly.

The Guangya says Du Zhong is also called Màn Yú; the Bowu Zhi says the bark of Du Zhong has silk-like threads inside that become visible when broken.
The Mingyi ji says: Du Zhong. One name: Si Zhong. One name: Mu Mian. Grows in Shangdang and Hanzhong. Gather the bark in the second, fifth, sixth, and ninth months.

Wu Pu says: Du Zhong. One name: Si Zhong. One name: Mu Mian. One name: Si Xian. [Source: Yulan.]

Du Zhong: flavor acrid, balanced. Governs pain in the lumbar spine; supplements the center; augments essence and qi; strengthens sinews and bones; fortifies the will; eliminates itching below the genitals, dribbling urination, and urinary residue. Long-term use lightens the body and resists aging. One name: Si Xian. Grows in mountain valleys.

The Mingyi ji says: one name Yuan [kite]. A parasite growing on mulberry trees in Hongnong; gather leaves on the third day of the third month and dry in the shade. The Shuowen says Yuan is a parasitic plant; the Odes say Yuan and female luo [lichen], or written as Jú; the Guangya says Wǎn Tóng is a parasitic plant. Also: Ji Ping and Ji Sheng [both meaning "parasitic growth"]. The Central Mountain Classic says the Dragon Mountain has many Xiě trees and Wǎn Tóng children; Guo Pu says it is the tree parasite, one name Niǎo; the Mao Odes say Yuan and female luo; the tradition says Yuan is a parasitic plant; Lu Ji says Xiě wood is a parasitic plant; also Yù Mù [lodging wood]; Guo Pu says Yù Tóng; it resembles the raspberry — red, black, sweet, and delicious.

Shennong Bencao Jing, Volume One

The Mingyi (Supplementary Physicians' Records) states: It is also known as Mujie (Stem Knot). It grows in Hanzhong and Wanju. The flowers are gathered in the fifth and tenth months; the roots are gathered in the tenth month and dried in the shade.

Examining the Daguan Bencao, it quotes the Donghuan Zhenren Yuan Shi Jing (Scripture of the Immortal Yuan Shi of East Florescence), which says: "I have climbed Mount Puwu and, tired of the fragrant herbs of gold and jade, I have rested in the correct way — this is the Five-加 (wu jia) plant." Lu Ding Gong's mother took Five-加 wine alone and thereby avoided death.

Manjing Shi (Vitex fruit): flavor bitter, slightly cold. It governs cold-heat painful obstruction in the spaces between sinews and bones, brightens the eyes, strengthens the teeth, benefits the nine orifices, expels white worms. Long-term use lightens the body and makes one resistant to aging. The fruit of small Vitex is equivalent. It grows in mountain valleys.

The Mingyi states: It grows on the southern slopes of Yangku in Henan, or around the high banks of Ping Shou Township, and in open fields. The fruit is gathered in the eighth and ninth months and dried in the shade.

Examining the Guangya: it says Mujing (male Vitex) and Manjing (trailing Vitex) are the same. The Guangzhi says: the Chu region calls it Jing; Mujing and Manjing are the same. Because the pronunciations of mu (牡) and man (蔓) are close, the Bencao Jing does not separately list the provenance of Manjing but incorporates it under Mujing, noting that it governs the five viscera, bodily cold-wind, head and brain pain, and beautifies the face; taken internally it descends qi, lightens the body, brightens the eyes, and increases longevity and resistance to aging. Another name is Xin Ke (per imperial citation, written as Kuan); another name is Hou Tao.

Xinyi (Magnolia bud): flavor acrid, warm. It governs the five viscera, bodily cold-wind, head and brain pain, and beautifies the face. Taken internally it descends qi, lightens the body, brightens the eyes, and increases longevity and resistance to aging. Another name is Xin Shen; another name is Hou Tao. It grows in river valleys.

Another name is Fang Mu. It grows in river valleys.

Examining the Han Shu: Yang Xiong's rhapsody says "listing Xinxiong among the thickets"; Shi Gu's commentary says Xinxiong is Xinyi. Tao Hongjing says: when young the bud is acrid and fragrant, which is what離駒 called Xinyi; Chen Cangqi records this.

Ma Xiang's commentary on Yang Xiong's rhapsody says "listing Xinxiong to flow as Yi"; the Han Shu commentary says Liuyi is the same as Xinyi (new-fresh); Xinxiong is Xinyi. Tao Hongjing says: when young its qi is acrid and fragrant, which is what 離駒 called Xinyi; Chen Cangqi records this.

It is said: when it first sprouts it resembles a writing brush; its flowers come earliest of all. Southerners call it Yingchun (Welcoming Spring); Tang people named it Yurui (Jade Pistil) and also Yulan (Jade Orchid).

Sang Shang Ji Sheng (Loranthus / Mistletoe on Mulberry): flavor bitter, balanced. It governs lumbar pain, stiffness of the back in children, carbuncles and swellings; it stabilizes the fetus, fills out the skin and flesh, strengthens the hair and teeth, promotes growth of beard and eyebrows. Its fruit brightens the eyes, lightens the body, and opens the spirit. Another name is Ji Xie; another name is Yu Mu; another name is Wan Tong. It grows in river valleys.

The Shuowen Jiezi says: "Fa" means the root of hair; "bi" means a hairpiece; "di" and "ti" are the same; or written as "di." The Book of Odes says: "Not worth wearing a hairpiece." Guan says: "Fa-ti is a hairpiece." The Book of Etiquette and Ceremony says: "The mistress of the house wears a xi (hairpiece)." The commentary says: "Being given a xi" is read as "bi-di" (a hairpiece). In ancient times, the hair of condemned criminals or those subjected to punishment was shaved off, or the hair of young boys was used. This Classic (Bencao Jing) would not tolerate using people's hair directly, so it used the trimmings left over from shaving. Some physicians have gone so far as to use the tianling gai (skull cap) to harmful effect, and even dried bones — none of this was done by the ancients.
Bi-fa (hairpiece) should be the shaved hair of a punished criminal, or the hair of a young boy according to Han dynasty scholars. It is the hair of a young boy. Li Dangzhi says it was used as an adornment, hence the name bi-di.

The above is one kind, same as the old classification.

Dragon Bone: flavor sweet, neutral. Primarily treats abdominal ghost-infestations, spirit possession, old demon influences, diarrhea, pus and blood in stool, vaginal discharge in women, hardened concretions and accumulations, and childhood heat with convulsions. Also treats convulsions and mania in both children and adults, qi binding below the heart causing inability to breathe, various abscesses, and kills spirit entities. Long-term use lightens the body, opens the spirit-mind, and extends life. Found in mountain valleys.
Wu Pu says: Dragon Bone is found in Jinди in mountain valleys near large rivers where water flows past. It is the bone of a dead dragon. The blue-white ones are best. Collected in the twelfth month or at any time. Dragon Bone fears dried lacquer and Sichuan pepper.
Lishi and Dragon Tooth: According to Shennong and Li's classification, greatly cold, treats convulsions and epilepsy; long-term use lightens the body. [See Imperial Daguan edition, this section.]
The Mingyi says: Dragon Tooth is found in Jindi and in the rocky waterside caves of Taishan where dragons have died. Collected at any time.
Note: The Fanzi Jiran says Dragon Bone comes from Hedong.

Musk (Chuixiang): flavor pungent, warm. Said to primarily break up foul qi, kill ghost-spirit entities, treat warm-malaria, gu-toxin (parasitic venom), epilepsy and tetanic spasm, and expel three worms. Long-term use eliminates evil influences and prevents oppressive nightmares. Found in mountain valleys.
The Mingyi says: Grows in Zhongtai and in Pengzhou and Yongzhou mountain regions; collected in spring when alive; the living substance is best.
Note: The Shuowen says: Musk deer resembles a small roe deer, with fragrant glands at the navel; it is a black-colored musk deer. The Erya quotes: "Chui" — the father is "chui," the feet are "chui." Guo Pu says: the feet resemble a musk deer and it has fragrance.

Cattle Gallstone (Niuhuang): flavor bitter, neutral. Primarily treats convulsions with chills and fever, high fever with mania and tetanic spasm. Eliminates evil and expels ghosts. Found in marshy lowlands.
