The Physicians' Records state: It is also called Du Lan; its bark resembles cinnamon and is fragrant; it grows in Lingling and Mount Tai. The bark is harvested in the twelfth month and dried in the shade.

Examining the Guangya: Mulan and Guilan are the same. Liu Kui's commentary on the Rhapsody of Shu Capital states that Mulan is a large tree whose leaves resemble those of evergreens; it blooms in winter and its fruit is like a small persimmon, sweet and delicious.

Southern people use it as plum; its bark can be eaten. Yan Shigu's commentary on the Han History states: the bark resembles roots in appearance and is fragrant, and can be used as a cosmetic preparation.

Huike: Flavor sweet, warm. Governs evil qi in the heart and abdomen, brightens the eyes, relieves red painful eyes with tearing. Long-term use lightens the body and augments qi so one does not feel hunger. Grows in river valleys. Long-term use prevents hunger.

Wu Pu states: Boke, also named Tu Shen. According to Shennong and Lei Gong: sweet, balanced, non-toxic. Grows in ponds and marshes; harvested in the eighth month. Supplements the center, strengthens the will, brightens the eyes. Grows in river valleys.

The Physicians' Records state: grows in Hangu and Baxi.

Examining the Shuowen: Jiao refers to white pepper; the Erya states jiao is a small shrub growing in clusters, with thorns; its fruit resembles an eardrop, purple-red, and can be spat out. The Yiqie Jing Yinyi states: the herbal classic renders it as ao; today's pepper seeds are precisely this.

Ju You (Citrus/Pomelo): Flavor acrid, warm. Governs phlegm-heat in the chest, counterflow qi; promotes movement of water and grain. Long-term use eliminates foul odors, descends qi, and opens the spirit. Also named Ju Pi (orange peel). Grows in river valleys. [Note: belongs to the Fruit category.]

Examining the Shuowen: Ju is a fruit from south of the Yangtze. You resembles the orange but is sour. The Erya states: in the states of Wu and Chu there is a tree called Yuan, with green bark, bearing fruit in winter; the fruit is red and the flavor is sour; one eats the skin and juice.

Kong [commentary]: the large is called Ju, the small is called You. The Tiaowenpian states that in Wu and Chu there is a tree called Luan, resembling the orange, sour-fruited, growing in Jiangnan. The Yugong states: their tribute included oranges and pomelos.

Those already accustomed to it lose their aversion to the illness. Sima Xiangru's rhapsody mentions oranges and pomelos. Zhang Yi states: You is the same as the orange (cheng), resembling the Ju but larger, sour in flavor, with thick skin.

The above Wood Upper-Grade items number twenty, of which nineteen are counted; the Ju You of the Fruit section should be included here.

Hair and Whiskers: Flavor bitter, warm. Governs the five types of urinary blockage, blockage of the passages, promotes urination and water pathways. Treats convulsions in children and tetanic stiffness in adults; spontaneously returns to and transforms through the spirit.

Red Rooster: Flavor sweet, slightly warm. Governs women's flooding and spotting, red and white vaginal discharge. Supplements deficiency, warms the center, stops bleeding, connects the spirit, kills toxins, and wards off inauspiciousness. The head governs killing demons. Those from the east gate are especially good.
The ribs govern deafness. The intestines govern enuresis. The crop lining governs diuresis. The white fat of the black hen governs wind-cold-damp impediment, the five slackenings and six urgencies, and stabilizes the fetus. The wing feathers govern stopping bleeding and blockage. The hen governs making amber-like objects. Removes heat, fire sores, and carbuncles; can be made into amber-like spirit objects. The white fat of the chicken grows in level marshes.

Wu Pu says: The red hen's egg can be made into amber-like objects.
The Mingyi says: It is produced in Joseon (Korea).
Regarding the Shuowen: "A domestic animal that knows the time." The character in the Jing is written as 雞. The ribs, intestines, large and small intestines, thigh flesh, the bird's gizzard, its droppings, its feathers and long feathers are all noted.

Wild Goose (Yan):
The fat, flavor sweet, balanced. Governs wind-induced contracture, clenching and acute one-sided withering, qi obstruction and poor circulation. Long-term use benefits qi, prevents hunger, lightens the body, and promotes longevity. Another name is Mu Fang (duck fat). Grows in pools and marshes.
Wu Pu says: Mu Fang — Shennong, Qibo, and Leigong say flavor sweet, non-toxic. Current editions should have the two characters "Mu Fang."
The Mingyi says: Produced in Jiangnan. Harvested at no fixed season.
Chong's Shuowen commentary says: Mu (鶩) is the Jiangnan goose. Guangya says: Goose is Mu; also called Jiaojing. Guo Pu says: Goose is also called Cang Yan.
According to the Shuowen: Today in Jiangdong, the domestic goose is also called Shu Fu (domesticated wild duck). The Fangyan says: East of the passes, geese are called Ge-e; in the outer regions of southern Chu, they are called Jiao or Cang Yan. The Liji says they come out like domesticated geese.
The entry for Jiu's fat also separately lists white duck and goose entries, which raises doubts that this refers to the wild goose. The character e (鵝) has no duck character; the character yan used for goose is the hurried pronunciation of yan. Therefore this goose fat entry is duck and goose fat, and should be written with the character Mu (鶩); the Mingyi did not understand this and listed it separately.

The above are two kinds of birds in the superior category, same as the old edition.

Wu Pu says: Ox Gallstone (Niu Huang) is bitter in flavor and non-toxic. When an ox is entering or leaving [a place] and moaning (the Yulan edition writes "those who have it"), at night it emits light (the Yulan edition writes "at night one can see its light"), and the ox runs about. The character "yu" is present. Inside the horn the ox dies; it enters the gallbladder, resembling a chicken egg yolk. [This is referenced in] the Hou Han Shu, in the biography of Yan Du, as a method.

The Mingyi says: It is produced in Jin region; it is obtained from oxen. Dry it in the shade for one hundred days; do not let it be exposed to sunlight or moonlight when processing.

Bear Fat (Xiong Zhi) is sweet and slightly cold in flavor. It governs wind impediment with loss of sensation, muscle spasms, accumulations and gatherings in the five viscera and abdomen, cold and heat, emaciation, head sores, white baldness, facial blotches and pustules. Long-term use strengthens the will, prevents hunger, lightens the body. It grows in mountain valleys.

The Mingyi says: It is produced in Yong Prefecture; collected in the eleventh month.

Commentary: Shuowen says that the bear is a beast resembling a pig that lives in the mountains and hibernates in winter.

White Glue (Bai Jiao) is sweet and balanced in flavor. It governs internal injury, extreme fatigue, pain in the lumbar region, emaciation, supplements the middle and boosts qi, closes the blood in women with no children, stops pain, calms the fetus. Long-term use lightens the body and prolongs life. Another name is Deer Antler Glue (Lu Jiao Jiao).

The Mingyi says: It is produced in Yun Zhong. Yun refers to the offering; it uses the hide or the antler.

Commentary: Shuowen says the glue from the courtyard is blue-white; ox glue when heated turns red. Zheng says: the so-called offering uses either the hide or the antler.

Glue

Donkey-hide Glue (E Jiao) is sweet and balanced in flavor. It governs collapse within the heart and abdomen, extreme fatigue with shivering as in malaria, pain in the lumbar and abdomen, aching of the four limbs, and bleeding in women. It calms the fetus. Long-term use lightens the body and boosts qi. Another name is Fu Zhi.

The Mingyi says: It is produced in Dongping Prefecture, made from the hide of the Lou ox, and comes from Dong'a.

Commentary: The two glues are not listed separately in the Bencao Jing as to their origins. It is suspected that the original Bencao Jing simply recorded "Glue," and that the Mingyi added the characters "White" and "E (Donkey-hide)" to separate them into two entries.

The above are six items from the upper grade of the Beasts category, same as the old edition.

The Eminent Physicians say: It grows in Wudu, in beehives among wood and stones.
A note from the Xijing Zaji (Miscellanies of the Western Capital) states that the King of Nanyue presented Emperor Gaozu with two hundred pieces of beeswax. The Yupian (Jade Chapters dictionary) says: "Wax is beeswax." Tao Hongjing says: White wax is produced within honey, hence it is called beeswax. The Shuowen (Explaining Writing) has no character for "la" (wax). Zhang You notes that "wei" is a separate character from "la," and that the original form was not "fen"; it has been amended here to "la" following that authority.

Oyster (Muli). Flavor: salty, balanced. Main uses: cold damage with alternating chills and fever, malarial shivers, fright, rage and anger; removes muscle stiffness and flaccidity, scrofulous sores; women's vaginal discharge, red and white. Long-term use strengthens the bones and joints, eliminates pathogenic qi, and prolongs life.
Named Muli; grows in ponds and marshes.

A note from the Shuowen: The li is a type of clam, resembling the li but somewhat larger, produced in the sea; people today eat them. Some sources say it is one of three kinds all born in the sea, belonging to the clam family, formed from thousand-year-old clams. The Qin [dynasty sources also mention this].
The Eminent Physicians say: Also called Muha (male clam); grows in the Eastern Sea; harvested at any season.

Tortoise Shell (Guijia). Flavor: salty, balanced. Main uses: flooding discharge of red and white fluids, breaking up masses and concretions, scabies and sores, the five hemorrhoids, genital erosion, damp impediment, heaviness and weakness of the four limbs, unclosed fontanelle in infants. Long-term use lightens the body and prevents hunger. Also called Divine House (Shenwu).
Grows in ponds and marshes.
The Eminent Physicians say: Grows in the Southern Sea and in lake waters; harvested at any season.
A note from the Guangya (Expanded Elegantiae): "Jie gui" means tortoise. Gao You's annotation to the Huainan [zi] says: "Gui ke" and "gui jia" are both terms for the tortoise shell.

Mantis Egg-case (Sangpiaoxiao). Flavor: salty, balanced. Main uses: internal injury, hernia and concretions, genital flaccidity, benefits essence and enables conception in women, blood occlusion, pain in the waist, the five urinary stranguries, promotes urination. Also called Shipi; grows on mulberry branches.
[Pertaining to the swallow section.]
Wu Pu says: The entry for Sangpiaoxiao — a second name is missing here — Shipi is omitted. Also called Haijiao. Also called Zhishen. According to Shennong: salty, non-toxic. [Verified from the Lan and Yu collections.]

Stone Honey (Shi Mi): Flavor sweet, nature balanced. Governs evil qi in the abdomen, all manner of fright and epileptic convulsions, calms the five viscera, replenishes all deficiencies, supplements qi, tonifies the center, relieves pain, resolves toxins, eliminates the hundred diseases, harmonizes all medicines. Long-term use strengthens the will and lightens the body.
One does not suffer hunger or age. Another name is Stone Malt Sugar (Shi Yi). Grows in mountain valleys.

Wu Pu says: Stone Honey — according to Shennong and Lei Gong, its qi is sweet and balanced, produced from river sources or river embankments; born [according to] Yulan, also citing one source, in the mountain valleys of Wudu.
The medical commentaries say: produced in the river sources of Wudu, among mountain rocks, white in color like paste — of excellent quality.
The Shuowen says: juan means sweet malt sugar; also called yuan-zi or written mi. The Classic of Mountains and Seas says: At Pingfeng Mountain there are many sandy rocks with beehives. Guo Pu says: the honey is from red bees.
The Xijing Zaji records: The King of Nanyue presented Emperor Gao with five hu of stone honey. The Pian says: juan and chong both mean sweet malt sugar. Su Gong says the character "stone" should be removed.

Bee Larva (Feng Zi): Flavor sweet, nature balanced. Governs swellings, wind in the head, eliminates gu toxins, supplements deficiency and emaciation, and damage to the center. Long-term use makes the skin luminous, complexion beautiful, and prevents aging. Large yellow bee larvae govern fullness and pain in the abdomen, and lighten the body with benefit.
Another name is Mason Bee Larva (Shi Feng Zi), also called Zhan Si. Grows in mountain valleys.
The medical commentaries say: produced in Wudu.
The Shuowen says: feng (蠭) is a flying insect that stings people. The old written form is written as lu. The Guangya says: feng...

The large ground-nesting wasp builds its chamber in the earth and is called the Earth Wasp (Shi Yao Weng). It stings and bites with its rostrum. The Liji refers to it as lang-ma-yao. Today in Jing and Ba regions it is called xian. Also the wood wasp — Guo Pu says it resembles the earth wasp but is smaller, nests in holes in trees, and in the Yan-Zhao region it is called yao-weng; the small ones...
In the Jiangdong region it is also called the wood wasp. Fangyan says: in the Yan-Zhao region the wasp is called feng. Zheng's commentary says fan is another term for yao. Also the wood wasp — Guo Pu says today the black wasp bores holes in bamboo and wood; some of these also have honey, and they are sometimes called di-shi (flute master). See yao...

Honey Ant (Mi Yi): Flavor sweet, slightly warm. Governs dysentery with pus and blood, supplements the center, continues severed injuries, heals metal wounds, supplements qi; one does not suffer hunger or age. Grows in mountain valleys.
The name fan is phonetically close; Sima Xiangru's Rhapsody uses ni for feng (maple). Zuo Zhuan — Guo Pu says today... The large ones with honey are called hu-yao; Guo Pu says fan is another form for yao. Zheng's commentary says fan is yao.

According to the Shuowen, it is written as "li" (鱧). The character "li" (鱧) is different from "li" (鱧), yet Mao Chang and Guo Pu used "huan" (鯇) to gloss "li" (鱧), which does not accord with Xu Shen. However, the Chuxue Ji quotes this passage also writing it as "li" (鱧). These two characters share the same pronunciation, which has led to errors and corruptions making it impossible to determine the details precisely. The Guangya also writes it as "li" (鱺), which is likewise a phonetic corruption. The Guangzhi says: "Tunyu has another name, huanlan yu." This is yet another divergent explanation. Lu Ji says: "Li (鱧) is the puffer fish (tai yu); Daoist practitioners consider it inauspicious because its head has star-like markings." Based on this, using "head" in the text as "li" (鱧) — the Guangya and the Bencao Yanyi take it to be black carp (hei li yu). If written with the character "li" (鯉), the Shuowen further takes it as "li" (鱧). The Guangzhi and the Bencao Yanyi say: li fish — people today call it black carp (hei li). Various explanations, if written with the character "li" (鱧), indicate that people in the eastern capital region still call it "ti yu." Also written as "li" (鱺), which is likewise a phonetic corruption.

Li Yu (Carp) Lard. The Mingyi says: flavor bitter, cold. It governs hot, red, painful eyes, blue-green blindness, and prolonged visual dimness. Long-term use strengthens the will and vital energy. It lives in ponds and marshes.

Commentary: The Shuowen says: li (鯉), also lú (鱸). The Erya says: li lú. The commentator Sheren says: li, another name lú. Guo Pu's note on li says: today this is the red carp (chi li yu); his note on lú says: a large fish resembling the li with bristles. The Shijing says "lú tong fa," the commentary says lú biǎn lǐ. From this we know Guo Pu distinguished them as two different fish. People in Yanzhou of today call red carp "chi li," call them "chi lü," call green carp "qing," call black carp "yuan ju," call white carp "bai hua," and call yellow carp "huang xiong."

The above are the superior-grade scaled fish, ten varieties in all, same as the old edition.

The Mingyi says: another name is Qian. It grows in Runan; harvested in the eighth month.

Commentary: The Shuowen says: Guo Pu says Qian means the root-stalk (fang, i.e., lotus rhizome). Also, its root is the lotus root (ou). The herb is called fuqu; the Erya says: he, furong (lotus). Guo Pu says its other name is furong; in Jiangdong people call it he, and also its seed-pod is called peng-ru.

The Physicians record: The egg of the mantis is collected in the second and third months and roasted over fire.
Commentary: The Shuowen [Jiezi] says it is the egg-case of the mantis, also written as "pi shao." The Erya says: "wu xie mao jiao" — the mantis egg case. The Erya also says it is not to be confused with the mantis itself; its young are called pi shao. Guo Pu says: another name is luojiao, being the egg of the mantis. Fan Zi Jiran says: pi shao comes from the three districts around the capital and fetches three hundred [cash] at the old price. The character "piao" has a similar sound and is an error. The Yupian says...

Commentary: The Shuowen says the jinjuhai [gold-curved sea shell] is what a hundred-year-old swallow transforms into, also called fu ling, transformed from an aged bat. The Erya calls it kui lu. Guo Pu says the Bencao describes its shape.
The Physicians record: It is produced in the South Sea. Shennong [classifies its taste as] bitter; Qibo [classifies it as] sweet; Bianque [classifies it as] salty. The large joints of the shell have markings like grinding teeth. It is collected at any season.
Wu Pu says: The sea clam — Shennong [classifies it as] bitter; Qibo sweet; Bianque salty. The large joints have markings like grinding teeth. Collected at any season.
The sea clam is bitter in flavor and balanced in nature. It governs coughing with counterflow of qi, panting, vexation and fullness, chest pain, and alternating cold and heat. Another name is kui ge.
[Same as luo (螺).]

The sea clam is round and thick with natural markings running lengthwise and crosswise — this is what is now called the cockle (han). The Rites of Zhou mentions the palace cook providing ge; Zheng Situ-Agriculture says this refers to lin ge [granary clam]; Du Zichun says lin shuai; the Zhou Shu [Book of Zhou states]...
One account says: the eastern sea clam has a hollow at the hole. The Yulan [encyclopedia] says: when pressing the clam, it is called han; it is listed separately under the sea clam entry, also named kui lu, also named huo dong fei.

Growing in river marshes.

The Mingyi states: Zhi Shi is bitter. Lei Gong says: sour, non-toxic. Li's [Canon]: greatly cold. Harvested ninth and tenth months, dried in the shade.

Commentary: Shuowen says: "Zhi is a tree resembling the orange." The Zhouli states: "When the orange crosses the Huai River it transforms into zhi." Shen Kuo's Mengxi Bitan states: "In the Six Dynasties period and before, medical prescriptions only used zhi shi; no one used zhi ke. Later people used the small, young fruit as zhi shi and the large as zhi ke."

Hou Po (magnolia bark): Flavor bitter, warm. Governs wind-stroke, cold damage, headache, alternating chills and fever, fright palpitations, qi and blood obstruction, dead muscle (anesthesia), eliminates three worms.

Wu Pu states: Hou Po — flavor bitter, warm, non-toxic. Li's [Canon]: slightly warm. Grows in Jiaozhi. Another name: hou po.

Mingyi states: Another name used by Shennong, Qi Bo, and Lei Gong — pu, non-toxic. The tree is called zhen. Guangya says: "Zhen bark is hou po." Also: "Double bark is hou po." Its seed is called zhu sheng. Fan Zi Ji Ran states: Hou Po comes from Hong Nong. By current popular usage, zhen is used as a vegetable; it is not clear whether this is correct.

Commentary: Shuowen says: "Pu is a tree." Zhen is a wood; the character is written with the wood radical.

Qin Pi (ash bark): Flavor bitter, slightly cold. Governs wind-cold marsh impediment, washing-washing chills, removes heat, blue-green nebula and white membrane in the eyes. Long-term use prevents the hair from turning white, lightens the body. Grows in valleys.

Wu Pu states: Qin Pi, also called Qin Pi. Astringent impediment, washing chills. Shennong, Lei Gong, Huangdi, Qi Bo: sour, non-toxic. Li's [Canon]: slightly cold. Or grows near water at Ku Ju. Harvested in the second and eighth months.

The seedling era: this is not truly the same thing. The Classic says: Tianmen Dong (Asparagus tuber) is also called Dian Le. Since "Le" and "Ji" are close in form, people today use this herb, which is not without reason.

Longan (Dragon Eye Fruit). Flavor: sweet, balanced. Main uses: treats evil qi of the five viscera, calms the mind, relieves poor appetite. Long-term use strengthens the hun-soul, sharpens hearing and eyesight, lightens the body, prevents aging, and opens the spirit. Also called Yi Zhi (Intelligence-boosting). Grows in mountain valleys.

Wu Pu says: Longan is also called Yi Zhi and Yao Shu, and also called Bi Mu. [Imperial citation]

The Famous Physicians say: the large ones resemble the Chinese hemp palm. They grow on pine trees in the South Sea region. Harvested in the fifth month and dried in shade.

Commentary from Guang Ya: Yi Zhi is longan. Liu Da's annotation to the Wu Du Fu says longan resembles lychee but is smaller and round like a pellet. Its flavor is sweeter than lychee. It is offered as tribute from the mountain valleys of Cangwu, Jiaozhi, and the South Sea.
People in the mountains also cultivate it.

The Famous Physicians say: flavor bitter and balanced. Main uses: treats anger and evil qi, stops night sweats and headache, and treats cold abscess conditions in women's yin region. Also called Nü Luo (Female Luo). Grows in mountain valleys.

Song Luo (Usnea lichen). Flavor: bitter, balanced. Main uses: treats anger and evil qi, stops night sweats and headache, treats cold abscess conditions in women's yin region. Also called Nü Luo. Grows in mountain valleys.

Commentary from Guang Ya: Nü Luo. The Mao Shi says: "Diao and Nü Luo together" — the commentary says Nü Luo is dodder. Lu Ji says: Song Luo twines up pine branches and is deep green, similar to dodder.

The Famous Physicians say: grows on Xiong'er Mountain.

Wei Mao (Euonymus alatus). Flavor: bitter, cold. Main uses: treats women's flooding and spotting with blood below the abdomen, treats fullness and sweating, dispels evil, kills ghost toxins and gu poison. Also called Gui Jian (Ghost Arrow). Grows in mountain valleys.

Wu Pu says: grows on Huo Mountain; harvested in the eighth month and dried in shade. Also called Wei Mao. Shennong, the Yellow Emperor, and Tong Jun all say: bitter, non-toxic; leaves resemble those of peach; shaped like feathers. Harvested in the first, second, and seventh months, dried in shade. Also grows in open fields. [Imperial citation]

The Famous Physicians say: Gui Jian is also called Shen Jian. Tao Hongjing says: its stems have three wing-like ridges shaped like arrow feathers.

Commentary from Guang Ya: Gui Jian is also called Shen Jian. Tao Hongjing says...

He Huan (Albizia, Silk Tree). Flavor: sweet, balanced. Main uses: calms the five viscera, benefits the heart and will. [The Imperial encyclopedia editions record it as harmonizing heart qi and the will and heart qi.] Makes people joyful and free from worry. Long-term use lightens the body, brightens the eyes, and fulfills one's wishes. Grows in mountain valleys.

The Mingyi [Supplementary Physicians' Records] states: Also called "Chicken's Foot" and "Kui Fruit." Grows in Hanzhong and Langye, Yanzhou district, Dongguo, and Chenxian county of Donghai. The fruit is harvested in the ninth and tenth months and dried in the shade.

Ziwei [Campsis grandiflora, Trumpet Creeper]: Taste is sour and salty (one edition records slightly cold). It governs women's postpartum residual ailments, uterine flooding, abdominal masses and accumulations, blood obstruction, alternating cold and heat, and emaciation. Grows in river valleys.

The emperor [note]: non-toxic. Resembles wheat-root and is black. Harvested in the first and eighth months, or found growing in Zhending. Also named Wuwei, Qumai, Lingjufu, Guimu, and Baihua. Shennong and Lei Gong classify it as sour; Qibo as acrid; Bian Que as bitter and salty; and [one note] yellow.

Wu Pu states: Ziwei.
Mingyi states: Also named Lingshao and Maihua. Grows in Xihai and Shanyang.

The Guang Ya [dictionary] says: This is the Weitiao Lingshao, also called Maiye. The Er Ya says: Shao is Lingshao. Guo Pu says: Also called Lingshi. The Bencao says it also has yellow flowers and fragrant white flowers. Guo Pu says: Shao has flowers. The names differ widely across sources.

Both the Guang Ya and the Tang Ben Zhu [Tang commentary] cite the term "Linglei" (a four-character phrase meaning Linglei Flower, produced in Sanfu). Lingji identifies it as mouse-tail grass, but this is probably wrong, so it has not been collected. Li Dangzhi says it is the root of Qumai, and according to Li's account it agrees with the Guang Ya.

Zhu Ling [Polyporus umbellatus, Pig Sclerotia]:
Wu Pu states: Zhu Ling is sweet and balanced in nature. It governs scabies and itching, resolves toxins, and eliminates [harmful influences]. Also named Xiangli. Taken long-term it lightens the body and prolongs the capacity for hard work in old age. Also called Jia Zhu Shi [pig dung]. Grows in mountain valleys. Resembles Fuling [Poria]. Harvested in the eighth month. Can treat thirst.

Mingyi states: Grows in Hengshan and Jiyinyan county. Also named Zhu Jian. Grows in river valleys.

The Zhuangzi and other texts say it is a type of zero-[fungus]. It grows in the mountain yin areas. Harvested in the second and eighth months; dried in the shade. The Zhuling root resembles a pig's testicle.

White Jujube Thorn [Bai Ji, Ziziphus spine]:
Taste is acrid and cold. Governs heart and abdominal pain, swellings and abscesses, rupture of pus, and relieves pain. Also named Ji Zhen [thorn needle]. Grows in river valleys.

Mingyi states: Also named Ji Ci [spine]. Grows in Yongzhou.

The Shuo Wen [dictionary] says: Ji is a small date that grows in thickets. The Er Ya says: Zi Zhan Ji [bristle jujube]. Some records say it is also called Bai Ji. Li Dangzhi says: This is the spine of the sour jujube tree. People today use Asparagus root [Tianmendong] instead.

Antelope Horn (羊角): Flavor: salty, cold. Main uses: brightens the eyes, boosts qi, arouses yang, dispels bad blood and downward flooding, wards off gu toxins, evil ghosts, and inauspicious influences, calms the heart qi, prevents nightmares and oppressive sleep. Grows in river valleys.
The Mingyi [Supplementary Physicians' Records] states: It grows at Shicheng and Huayin Mountain. Collected at any time.

Commentary: The Shuowen says: "Li is a large sheep with slender horns." The Guangya says: "Beautiful hide, cool horns." The Erya says: "The ling is a large sheep." Guo Pu says: "The ling sheep resembles a sheep but with large, round, sharp horns, preferring to live on mountain cliffs." Tao Hongjing says: The Erya name is shan. The Guangya says beautiful hide and cool horns. The Erya says the ling is a large sheep. Guo Pu says the shan resembles the Wu-sheep but with large horns projecting outward.
In western regions it is called bi, the correct character in the Bencao Classic is ling, which is in fact the character li written in common form. This should properly be written li. Guo Pu's Erya commentary says: the shan resembles the Wu-sheep but with large horns projecting outward.

Rhinoceros Horn (犀):
The Mingyi states: Grows in Yongchang and Yizhou.
Flavor: bitter, cold. Main uses: counters the hundred toxins, worm infestations, evil ghost miasma qi, kills the poisons of gou-wen plant, zhen-feather poison, and snake venom; eliminates confusion, delusion, and oppressive dreams. Long-term use lightens the body. Grows in mountain valleys.

Commentary: The Shuowen says: "The rhinoceros is an ox from south of the frontier, with one horn on the nose and one horn on the top of the head, resembling a pig." The Erya says the rhinoceros resembles a domestic pig. Guo Pu says: It looks like a water buffalo with a pig's head, large belly, and short legs.
It has three hooves, is dark in color, and has three horns — one on the nose, one on the top of the head, one on the forehead; the one on the nose is the feeding horn, small and not projecting outward; it likes to eat thorns. There are also single-horned varieties. The Shanhai Jing says: On Gu Mountain there are many white rhinoceroses. Guo Pu says: These are all different species from the bi-cold, chu-nu, bi-chen, bi-shu, and other types of rhinoceros horns. Fan Zi Ji Ran says rhinoceros horn comes from Nanjun.
Top grade priced at eight thousand, middle grade at three thousand, lower grade at one thousand.

The above: seven items of medium-grade animal substances, same as the old [classification].

Xi (熙) Dung: Flavor: acrid, neutral. Main uses: treats gu toxins, ghost-possession ailments, expels inauspicious qi, breaks the five types of urinary obstruction, promotes urination. Grows in level valleys.
The Mingyi states: Grows on high mountains.
Commentary: The Shuowen says: The swallow (yan) is the primordial bird; it holds cloth in its mouth and distributes it to branch-ends; its tail is like the character for "elephant" (象); it builds nests and avoids the days wu and ji; it is the primordial bird; the people of Qi and Lu call it yi; the name comes from its own call; the character is shaped like the bird's form, also written as [alternate form].

White Horse Penis: flavor salty, nature balanced. Governs injury to the center, severed pulse, inability of the yin organ to rise, strengthens the will, benefits qi, grows muscle and flesh, fattens and strengthens, produces offspring. Eyes govern fright and epilepsy, abdominal fullness, and festering sores; when slaughtered it is used medicinally. The beard and hooves govern [related conditions].
Egret [herb]: dispels evil qi, scrofula sores, difficult lactation, wards off injury, evil qi, ghost toxins, and gu-poison infestations and inauspicious influences. Grows in flat marshes.
Physicians say it grows in Yunzhong.
Velvet Deer Antler: flavor sweet, warm. Governs bleeding downward of bad blood, cold and heat, fright and epilepsy; benefits qi, strengthens the will, grows teeth, and prevents aging. The hardened antler governs malignant sores, carbuncles and swellings, drives out evil and malign qi, and stagnant blood in the yin region.
Physicians say: the velvet is taken in the fourth or fifth month when the antlers are shed, dried in the shade, and used when dry; the antlers are taken in the seventh month when they are in velvet.
Annotation from Shuowen: the eel antler ... closes downward blocking blood, treats blood accumulations, blood pain, women's vaginal discharge, and replenishes the marrow, fills the bone marrow; long-term use increases longevity and the fat can be used as a medicinal.
Ox Horn Core: flavor salty, warm. Governs blue-green blindness of the eyes, kills itch mites, stops cold diarrhea, wards off evil ghosts and fierce tigers and wolves, stops fright palpitations; long-term use calms the heart, benefits qi, lightens the body. Grows in river valleys.
Physicians say it grows in Hexi and is collected at any time.
Ram's Horn: flavor salty, warm. Governs blue-green blindness, kills itch mites, stops cold diarrhea, wards off evil ghosts, tigers, and wolves, stops fright palpitations; long-term use calms the heart, benefits qi, lightens the body. Grows in river valleys.
Annotation from Shuowen: "Gu" refers to a summer ram; the male is called "Gu." Erya says: the female sheep is called "Gu." Guo Pu says: nowadays people simply use "Zhu" and "Gu" as the names for black and white sheep.
Male Dog Penis: flavor salty, balanced. Governs injury to the center, yin flaccidity with inability to rise, enables strength and endurance, produces offspring, removes the twelve diseases of women's vaginal discharge. Another name is "Dog Essence Fat," which governs brightening the eyes.
Physicians say: collected on the first day of the Fufu period in the sixth month and dried in the shade for one hundred days.

Crab: flavor salty, cold. Governs evil qi and heat accumulation with pain in the chest, facial distortion and swelling. Burning [the shell] drives away mice. Grows in ponds and marshes.

The Shuowen says: found in the waters of the Yi and Luo rivers; collected at any time. The Mingyi says: produced in the Yi and Luo rivers; collected without a fixed season.

The Shuowen says: the clam (bang ge) has no fixed abode. The Erya says: the small clam is the luo (螺). Guo Pu says: it is also called the bie shao (鱉蛸); it resembles a crab but is smaller.

The Shuowen says: [the crab] has two large claws and eight legs, moves sideways, is not a snake or eel. The Erya says: crabs have six joints and two pincers.

Cicada shell: flavor salty, cold. Governs childhood fright epilepsy, night crying, epileptic disorders, and alternating cold and heat. Grows on willow trees.

The Shuowen says: in the fifth month the millet dries out [at the same time the cicada sings].

The Mingyi says: the cicada is the one that sings from exertion.

The Shuowen discusses the various names and pronunciations of the cicada, noting it is also called fu chan (伏蟬) and sang ci (桑蛓); the Zhou Rites Artificer's Record refers to "zuo chan," and Zheng Xuan reads zuo as the sound "zha zha," meaning a loud external sound. The Shuowen glosses it as meaning "great."

The cicada's pronunciation is the same as zuo; the old text wrote it as pi chan. The Bielu says: the singing one is the ming chan (鳴蟬); its shell is also called wu (梧).

Various regional dialects have different names for types of cicada (jie chan, etc.), as recorded in the Shiming, Fangyan, and other sources. The Bencao Jing's Tao Hongjing gives variant pronunciations.

The cicada referred to in the Monthly Ordinances as the "cold-cicada" is identified in the Erya as pi kuai (蚍夬); the Tang edition's note disputes this.

Maggot (qi cao): flavor salty, slightly warm. Governs bad blood, blood stasis, blood clots, swelling and abscesses, broken bones with blood accumulation below the ribs, hard fullness and pain, menstrual blockage, clouding of the eyes with superficial opacities and white membranes. Also called du chan (蠹蟬). Found growing [in the earth].

[On the swallow:] The Erya calls the swallow "fu"; the Xiazheng says it arrives in the second month, descending — the swallow then gazes about. The commentary says the swallow is the "yi" [second Heavenly Stem]. In the ninth month it ascends; the "yuan bird" — the commentary says the yuan bird is the swallow.

Bat Droppings: Flavor acrid, cold. Mainly treats facial abscesses and swellings, skin that feels washed with pain, intestinal bleeding, breaks up accumulations of cold and heat, disperses fright palpitations. Also called "shuyuan," also called "shigan." Grows in mountain valleys.

The Mingyi says: produced at Hepu; harvested in the tenth and twelfth months.

Hedgehog Skin: Flavor bitter, balanced. Mainly treats the five hemorrhoids, genital erosion, bleeding of red and white and five-colored discharge that will not stop, swelling and pain of the genitals radiating to the back, killed by cooking in wine. Grows in river valleys.

The Mingyi says: grows in the hills and fields of Chu; harvested at any time.

According to the Shuowen and Erya: [the hedgehog] resembles the porcupine; sometimes written as "gua." The Guangya says it is the "tiger king hedgehog." The Erya says its fur has spines. Guo Pu says that today it is described as mouse-shaped. The Huainanzi's "Shunxun" chapter...

Wasp Nest: Flavor bitter, balanced. Mainly treats fright epilepsy and convulsions, cold and heat, evil qi, seizure disorders, possession by ghosts, gu poison, intestinal hemorrhoids; excellent for fire-heat conditions. Also called "fengchang." Grows in mountain valleys.

[Note:] Inside the gull's droppings there is a hedgehog.

The Mingyi says: also called "baichuan," also called "fengqiao." Grows on sheep-柯; harvested on the seventh day of the seventh month; dry in the shade.

According to the Huainanzi's Xunlun chapter: a wasp nest cannot contain eggs. Gao You's commentary says: the nest is a hive.

Basket [creature] innards: Flavor salty, balanced. Mainly treats concretions and conglomerations in the abdomen, hard accumulations, alternating cold and heat, removes masses, flesh polyps, genital erosions, hemorrhoids, and malignant flesh. Grows in marshes and ponds.

The Mingyi says: produced at Danyang; harvested at any time.

Commentary from the Shuowen: the horseshoe crab's skin is called "hao," and can be used to make drums. The water insect resembles a gecko and grows large quickly. Tao Hongjing says: the tuo is the shell of the lu.

Chujī (Ailanthus silkworm): bitter, neutral in nature. It governs heart and abdominal evil qi, impotence, and benefits the essence; strengthens the will, promotes fertility, improves complexion, supplements the center, and lightens the body. It grows in river valleys.

The Physicians say: it is found on ailanthus trees in Henei. Collected in the seventh month and sun-dried.

Commentary: the Guangya says the chujiu is the chujī. The Erya says: lun, the heavenly chicken—Guo Pu says it is a small insect with a black body and red head, also called shājī, or alternately chujī.

The Shijing says: in the sixth month the shājī beats its wings. Lu Ji says: the shājī resembles a butterfly but has spotted, multi-layered wings that are bright red; it is sometimes called the "heavenly chicken." In the sixth month it flies and beats its wings.

It makes a rustling sound. The people of Youzhou call it pucuo—this is the same creature.

Huó qūqiāo: salty, cold in nature. It governs bandit wind, retching, stiffness of the sinews, loss of liver function, fright impediment, and spasms and contracture. Another name is língtū; it lives in ponds and marshes.

The Physicians say: another name is shìqiāo; another name is fùqiāo, found on great mountains and in shaded, sandy embankments; collected in the eighth month.

Commentary from the Shuowen: qiāo is a type of snail creature. Ying is another name for the snail shell. The Guangya says: the liying and qiāo-ox and mou-qiāo. The Zhongshan Classic says: Mount Qingyao has many pú-qiāo; Guo Pu says: pú-qiāo is another name for the ox-snail. The Physicians list the snail-ox separately.

[The passage on the qiāo insect and snail references the Shuowen, the Zhouli, and the Erya regarding various names and rites, concluding that it is also called xīyì and lives in river valleys.]

Stone Dragon Lizard (Scincus): salty, cold in nature. It governs evil qi of the five viscera, breaks up stone-strangury, stops bleeding below, and promotes urination and water passages. Also called shǒugōng (wall gecko), also called shíyì (stone skink), also called shí lóngzǐ.

Wu Pu says: the stone dragon is also called mountain dragon-child, also called shǒugōng, also called stone skink. It is found in Pingyang and in the rocky hills of Jingshan. Collected in the fifth month, placed on stones, and dried.

Physicians' note: Also named Panjì, also named Dūnjì. Found in the interior of He (Henei), taken from manure and compost heaps around human dwellings; those that move backward are the best.

Commentary citing the Shuowen: The character zào (竈) refers to dung beetles (qiānglàng). The Guangya says: wánhuí, cáo, and dung beetles are all the same creature; the qiānglàng and its variant names are noted in the Erya. The soil of dung heaps is where these creatures — called qiān and sāo and qiānglàng — are found, though in different localities different names are used. The Mao Shi (Odes) says: the cricket resembles the qiānglàng; the Commentary says it lives in wood; variant names from eastern dialects are given. The Liezi, "Tianrui" chapter, says the wūzú creature produces the qiānglàng; its shell in the Liang-Yi region is called chán; it moves on its back, swiftly on foot. The Shuowen has no character péng; the character dù is borrowed for it by phonetic resemblance; the character chí is a scribal error.

The root of the qiānglàng: the Bowuzhi (Records of Diverse Matters) states: it is used to treat vaginal bleeding, reddish-white discharge, stoppage of menstrual blood, swelling and pain in the lower yin region, fever and chills, boils and scrofula, infertility; found in pools and marshes.

Physicians' note: Found in the East Sea; gathered at any season.

Cuttlefish bone: flavor salty, mildly warm. Governs: palpitations, concretions and accumulations, persistent hard masses, alternating cold and heat, heavy uterine bleeding and five-colored vaginal discharge in women, pain drawing from the lower abdomen to the genitals, sores, scabies, dead flesh. Found in pools and marshes.

Commentary citing the Shuowen: jì — the cuttlefish — also written as lǐ; the Zuo Si rhapsody mentions the "ink fish." Liu Da's annotation says the cuttlefish has ink inside its belly. Tao Hongjing says this creature is a transformation of the seagull.

Physicians' note: Found in Yingchuan; gathered in the fourth month, taking only those that have died naturally.

White silkworm (dead and stiff): flavor salty. Governs: fright and epilepsy in children, night crying, expels the three worms, removes dark spots and blemishes, makes the complexion good; treats male genital sores. Found in flat marshes.

Note: The mated worm also produces offspring; after mating, the silkworm loses its eyebrows and eyes, is easily injured. Collected and processed; the Yupian writes it as cán zào. It should properly be written as jiāng (stiffened); the character yǒng (奮) is incorrect.

Commentary citing the Shuowen: zào means "producing silk." The Huainanzi, "Shuilin Xun" chapter states: the silkworm eats but does not drink; after twenty-two days it transforms. The Bowuzhi says the silkworm transforms three times; it conceives before mating and after mating does not [continue to eat — text breaks off].

Dried fish (bào yú) scales: flavor pungent, mildly warm. Governs: palpitations, concretions and accumulations, persistent hard masses, alternating cold and heat, heavy uterine bleeding and five-colored vaginal discharge in women, pain drawing from the lower abdomen to the genitals, sores, scabies, dead flesh. Found in pools and marshes.

Gu (Shennong Bencao Jing, Tang edition note): People in Hanzhong eat it to move qi downward. It is called Shican (stone silkworm), also known as Lufei, also known as Fupan. Formerly written as Lian; the Shu commentary cites this and writes it as Lian.

Wu Pu says: Flavor salty, cold. It governs cold and heat in the abdomen and chest, washing sensations, blood accumulation, concretions and conglomerations, breaks up hard masses, promotes the discharge of blood stasis, and facilitates childbirth. An excellent remedy. Also named Dibie (ground turtle). Grows in rivers and marshes.

The Mingyi (Supplementary Physicians) says: Also called Tubi. Found in Hedong and sandy places, under the walls of people's homes, in damp underground spots. Dried in the sun in the tenth month.

Examination: The Shuowen says it belongs to the Fei category of insects. The Guangya says it is also called Fufei. Guo Pu says it is the same as Changyang. The Mao Shi (Book of Odes) says: "The grass insects chirp" — the commentary says they resemble locusts in varying sizes, with a peculiar sound, greenish color, and like to live among taro plants.

Fuyi (bat): Flavor salty, balanced. It governs dim vision, enabling one to see clearly at night with keen eyesight. Long-term use makes people cheerful and free from worry. Also named Bianfu. Grows in river valleys. Formerly classified under the Birds section, now moved.

Wu Pu says: Fuyi sometimes lives in people's homes. After the Beginning of Summer (Lixia), dry it in the shade. Treats dim vision and enables people to see in the night with a luminous clarity. The Wen Lei classifies Bianfu as living in river valleys.

The Mingyi says: Found on Mount Tai and in people's houses. Harvest after the Beginning of Summer and dry in the shade.

Examination: The Shuowen says it is the Bianfu. The Guangya says Fuyi, Feishu (flying mouse), Xianshu (immortal mouse), and Yougong are all the same. The Erya says Bianfu is also called Fuyi. The Fangyan (Dictionary of Regional Expressions) says: west of the passes, in the Qin and Long regions, it is called Bianfu.

East of the passes: Li Dong's text says it is the Tianshu (sky mouse), also called Feishu or Xianshu. West of the passes, in the Qin and Long regions, it is called Bianfu.

The insect section refers to it as Fuyi, or as the insect Fuyi, also called Laoshu (old rat) or Xianshu (immortal mouse). The Erya classifies Bianfu as Fuyi. The Fangyan says north of the passes, the Yan region calls it Fei.

The above medium-grade entries in the Insects and Fish section total seventeen kinds; formerly sixteen kinds. Examination: the Fuyi from the Birds section should be moved here.

Meireal (plum fruit): Flavor sour, balanced. It governs descending qi, eliminating heat and vexing fullness, calming the mind, pain in the limbs, hemiplegia, loss of sensation, dead flesh; removes dark blemishes and treats malign diseases. Grows in river valleys.

Wu Pu says: Plum fruit — as recorded in the Daguan Bencao, it brightens the eyes and boosts qi. The Wu clan's Bencao and the Daguan Bencao cite it for removing dark blemishes and treating malign diseases. Grows in river valleys.

Wu Pu states: Wutou is also named Langdang, Qiandi, Dugong, Beifuguo [variant: Beiguo]. Another name is Gengzi. Shennong, Lei Gong, Tong Jun, and Huangdi: sweet, has toxicity. It begins growing in the first month; the leaves are thick, the stems grow in fours opposite each other, resembling artemisia. It resembles the head of a crow with two prongs joined together like a crow's beak, hence the name Wuhui. In the tenth month the fruit is reddish; Li's [classification]: greatly cold. In the eighth month it turns red; dry in the shade. This is the large-angled form of Fuzi (accessory root).

Also stated: Wuhui — Shennong, Lei Gong, Tong Jun, Huangdi: has toxicity. Li's [classification]: slightly cold. In the tenth month the shape resembles a crow's head with two prongs joined like a crow's beak, hence it is named Wuhui.

The counteractions and incompatibilities are the same as Wutou. One name is Jianzi, another is Langzi. Shennong and Qibo: greatly toxic. Li's [classification]: greatly cold. In the eighth month dry in the shade. This is the large-angled form of Fuzi.

The avoidances and counteractions are the same as Fuzi. [Original text and commentary follow.]

The Mingyi [Additional Physicians] record: grows on the north side, in the second month the fruit turns red. Dry in the shade. When it grows to three cun or more it becomes Tianxiong. Guo Pu says: it is the same as Wutou; in the east of the Yangtze it is called Langcao. Fan Zi Ji Ran says: Wutou comes from the Sanfu region; the white ones — according to Shuowen, grown in the north. Zhaozhou says it is the Langcao plant. Guo Pu says it is Wutou. Huainanzi Zhushu Xun says: nothing is more dangerous than chicken poison. Gao You's commentary says: chicken poison is Wutou. Note on chickens —

The Guoyu says: Li Ji placed aconite in the meat — "jun" refers to the seedling of this plant. Zhaozhou says it is the Langcao plant. The Mingyi list Cezu (lateral accessory root) as a separate entry, which is incorrect.

The toxicity: what is called "laughing toxin" is also the same as Qianzhuzi and Cezu. The Mingyi listing of Cezu as a separate entry is incorrect.

Tianxiong (Tall Aconite): Flavor pungent, warm. Governs major wind, cold-damp impediment, pain in all the joints, cramping and contracture, breaks up accumulations of evil qi, metal wounds; strengthens sinews and bones, lightens the body, makes one tireless in walking. Also named Baimu. Imperial commentary cites: "Grows yin qi."

Without fatigue, strengthens the will, causes people to increase in martial strength. [Variant of the black-text edition:] grown from strength.

The Mingyi state: grows at Shaoshi [mountain]. In the second month gather the roots, dry in the shade.

Note: The Guangya says: Quju, Tudu, and Fuzi — at one year it is Qianzhuzi; at two years it is Wuhui; at three years it is Fuzi; at four years it is Wutou; at five years it is Tianxiong. [As cited in] the Huainanzi Jing —

Shen Nong's Classic of Materia Medica, Volume 3

[On Jiegeng (balloon flower root):] The Shuowen says: Jiegeng is the name of a medicine. The Guangya says it resembles jiegeng. The Zhanguo Ce says: "Today one seeks bupleurum and finds it by the tomb of Liang's father in the shadow of Que, loading it by the cartful." [But] jiegeng found in marshy lowlands will not be obtained even after many generations. The Erya says: tulu, tulou. Guo Pu says: it resembles qi. According to the Mingyi [Records], this is an alternate name; below there is also a separate tulu entry — but this is not correct.

[Feihao zi (a plant):] Flavor bitter, cold. It governs toothache, expels worms, [treats] flesh sores and cramping, enables a person to walk vigorously, causes one to see ghosts; eating too much makes a person run wildly. Long-term use lightens the body, enables one to run as fast as a galloping horse, strengthens the will, increases strength, and penetrates the spirit. Another name is Hengtang. Grows in river valleys.

The physician's record says: another name is Cifei lan [orchid]. Tao Hongjing says that nowadays apothecaries mostly write it as henjì [thistle], the old form being song.

The Shuowen has no entry for the characters song or hui; the Shiji, in the biography of Chunyu Yi, says...

The Guangya says: Cipei lan orchid. Another name Cixing tang; grows on seashores and in Yongzhou; harvest the seeds in the fifth month.

[A story:] When a noblewoman of Chuanchuan carried a child but could not give birth, she drank [a preparation of] langdang [henbane]; one source in the Bencao Tujing quotes this as langdang.

[Caohao (Artemisia/wormwood):] Flavor bitter, cold. It governs mange and itching, malignant sores, kills insects, expels persistent heat lodged in the joints, and brightens the eyes. Another name is Qinghao; another name is Fangkui. Grows in rivers and marshes.

The physician's record says: grows at Huayin.

The Shuowen says: hao [wormwood], gu [drum]. Commentary and phonetic notes say hao may also be written as lian. The Erya says: hao, gu. Tao Hongjing says: this is today's qinghao; those in the middle of it used for moxibustion with a fragrant smell are gu. The Shiji, in the biography of Sima Xiangru...

[Xuanfu hua (inula flower):] Flavor salty, warm. It governs bound qi, fullness below [the heart], fright palpitations, removes water, opens the five viscera, resolves cold and heat, supplements the middle, and descends qi. Another name is Jinfeicao; another name is Shenghú. Grows in river valleys.

The physician's record says: another name Daihu; grows in flat marshes; harvest the flowers in the fifth month; dry in the sun for twenty days until done.

The Shuowen says: xuanfu is daogeng. The Erya says: xuanfu is daogeng. Guo Pu says: xuanfu resembles chrysanthemum.

Rhubarb (Da Huang). Flavor: bitter; nature: cold. It principally treats blood stasis, blood blockage with alternating chills and fever, breaks up concretions, accumulations and gatherings, retained fluids and undigested food; it purges and cleanses the intestines and stomach, expels the old and brings forth the new, and frees the passage of water and grain. [The original has the character "Dao" (道).] Below this: regulates the center and promotes digestion. It is at peace with and harmonizes the five viscera. Grows in mountain valleys.

Wu Pu says: flavor bitter, non-toxic; Bian Que [says] bitter, non-toxic; Li's [school says] slightly cold — it is called "General-in-Chief." It grows either in Shu Commandery's northern district or in Long-xi. In the second month flowers appear; the leaves grow red, in sets of four opposite pairs, the yellow artemisia grows to a height of about three feet; in the third month the flowers are yellow, in the fifth month the fruit is black; roots are gathered in the third month — the roots have a yellow juice. Slice and dry in shade.

The Mingyi says: another name is Huang Liang; it grows in He-xi and Long-xi; roots are gathered in the second and eighth months and dried over fire.

Pharmaceutical [note]: The Guangya says "Huang Liang" means the same thing.
[Pharmaceutical note]: The Lanlan section formerly rendered Ting Ting Lan. [Imperial edition.]

Tingli (Lepidium/Descurainia seed). The Guangya says: [Imperial edition.]
The Mingyi says: another name is Xia Li; another name is Guang Hao; gather the fruit after the beginning of summer, dry in shade; it goes well with wine.

Tingli: the Shuowen says it is a grass called Xia Li; the Guangya says it is Gou Hao; it grows at Da Shi; Tingli is also [mentioned in the] Erya; Guo Pu says the fruit and leaves both resemble mustard; the Huainanzi, "Miaocheng Xun" chapter says [something about it].

Tingli cures puffiness/swelling [Zhang]; the Xijing Zaji says Tingli dies in the height of summer.

Balloon Flower root (Jie Geng). Flavor: acrid; nature: slightly warm. It principally treats pain in the chest and flanks as if stabbed by a knife, abdominal fullness, intestinal rumbling with a hollow sound, fright, fear, and palpitations. [Imperial Encyclopedia citation; original text printed in black characters.] Another name: Li Ru; another name: Fang Tu; another name: Bai Yao; another name: Geng Cao; another name: Qi Ju. Grows in tall artemisia thickets; roots are gathered in the second and eighth months and sun-dried.

Wu Pu says: sweet, non-toxic; Li's [school says] greatly cold; the leaves resemble those of Qi Ju, like the tube of a zheng [instrument], purplish-red; sprouts in the second month. [Imperial Encyclopedia edition.]

Lei Gong says: Jie Geng — another name Fu Di; another name Bai Yao; another name Li Ru; another name Lu Ru. Shennong [says] harmonizing, bitter, non-toxic; Bian Que, Huangdi [say] salty; Qi Bo [says] —

The Mingyi says: another name Li Ru; another name Fang Tu; another name Bai Yao; another name Geng Cao; another name Qi Ju. Grows in tall artemisia thickets; roots are gathered in the second and eighth months and sun-dried.

The Guangya dictionary says: "Yuanwei" is the same as Shegan (Belamcanda chinensis). In the Xunzi's chapter "Encouraging Learning" it says: "In the west there is a tree called Shegan, its stem four inches long." Fan Zi Ji Ran says the root of Shegan is like [a snake].

Shé (Snake) — the combined character is the word "cāng." [Place: ] Anding.
[Two characters unclear] — Guangsha says: combined.
The Mingyi [Famous Physicians] records: grows in Yizhou; harvested in the eighth month; dried in shade.
According to the Bencao Tujing: some say this is Quepiào (sparrow gourd), which is actually another name for Luómo (Metaplexis japonica). According to Lu Ji, Yuanlan is another name for Luómo; people in Youzhou call it Quepiào, which is the same as the "lǐ" in the Erya. Yuanlan is also found in Tang Bencao, listed separately under Luómo; it is not the same as Nüqing.
Flavor: bitter; nature: cold. Main uses: cold damage with fever, malarial fever, ghost toxin, phlegm accumulation in the chest causing vomiting and reflux. Another name: Hucao. Grows in river valleys.

Hengshan (Dichroa febrifuga)
Wu Pu says: Hengshan is also called Qiye. Shennong and Qibo say it is bitter; Li's classification: greatly cold; Tongjun says it is acrid and toxic. Harvested in the second and eighth months.
The Mingyi records: grows in Yizhou and central Han; roots harvested in the eighth month; dried in shade.
Note: In the Hou Han Shu, the biography of Hua Tuo says Tuo transmitted the Qiye Qingzhan Powder (Lacquer-leaf and Qingzhan Powder): one dou of lacquer leaf shavings and fourteen liang of qingzhan — this is the standard formula. It is said that long-term use eliminates the three worms and benefits the five viscera.

Shu Qi (Dichroa febrifuga aerial parts)
Flavor: acrid; nature: balanced. Main uses: treating epilepsy, rebellious ascending qi, chills and fever, abdominal masses and accumulations, evil qi, qingzhan, ghost toxin. [Note: "zhù" is written as "dǎn" in some editions.] Grows in river valleys.
Wu Pu says: grows as the leaf of Shu Qi; another name is Hengshan. Shennong, Qibo, and Leigong say it is acrid and toxic; the Yellow Emperor says it is acrid; one tradition says it is sour, resembling lacquer leaves and blue-green菁, similar in appearance; harvested in the fifth month.
The Mingyi records: grows in the Jiangling mountains and in the Shu-Han region of central China; it is the sprout of Changshan; leaves harvested in the fifth month and dried in shade.
Note: the Guangya says Hengshan is Shu Qi. Fan Zi Ji Ran says Shu Qi comes from Shu commandery.

Veratrum album (Lilu)

Lilu (Veratrum / false hellebore): Taste: acrid, cold. Primary uses: gu-toxin, cough with counterflow qi, diarrhea and intestinal flux, head sores, scabies and itching, malignant sores; kills all gu-parasites and toxins; removes dead flesh. Another name: Cong Ran. Grows in mountain valleys.
It is salty and toxic. Wu Pu says: Lilu — another name is Cong Kui, another name is Feng Lu, another name is Hui Kui. [御覽 citation:] Also called Gong; also called Shan. Shennong and Leigong say it is acrid and toxic. Huangdi says it is toxic. [Qi Bo adds further notes.]
Wu Pu says: another name is Cong Kui; grows on Tai Shan. The Fan Zi Ji Ran says: Lilu comes from Hedong; the yellow-white variety is best. The Erya says: E — mountain onion — grows on Tai Shan. Roots harvested in the third month, dried in the shade. Small [rootlets] connect; roots harvested in the second month.

The Mingyi says: another name is Cong Kui; another name is Shan Cong, grows on Tai Shan. Bianque says it is bitter, toxic, and greatly cold. Leaf and root. [The Yulan] also gives names Gong and Shan.

Gou Wen (Gelsemium / heartbreak grass):
[The Yulan] records an alternate name.

Wu Pu says: Qin Gou Wen — another name is Du Gen (poison root). Taste: acrid, warm. Primary uses: metal-weapon wounds, breast abscesses, chest obstruction, malign wind, cough with counterflow qi, edema; kills ghost-infixation [parasitic spirits causing disease].

The Mingyi says: Grows on Fu Gao mountain and in Kuaiji; roots harvested in the first month.

[Case:] The Guangya says: Tu Si (dodder) is also called Cong Ji.

The Mingyi says: Grows on Fu Gao mountain, and according to the Huainan Zi commentary, if a viper bites a person and you apply this with water-shield (Brasenia), it will heal. People in Gaomen call it "Wen Zang"; it is also called Ye Ge (wild kudzu) from the Ling [mountains]. [Gou Wen is deadly.]

The root [section from] Guangya says: Grows on Fu Gao mountain; the Huainan Zi — Lin Xun chapter — says if a viper bites a person and you apply it with water-shield it heals. People in Gaomen call it "吻葬 (wen zang)" and also call it Wild Kudzu from the mountain range. Kougui (桂心) with onion leaves.

Southerners call it Hu Man; the common name is Duan Chang Cao (intestine-severing herb). This plant is extremely toxic; it is not used medicinally. It is feared that the one listed in the materia medica is a different substance — not this Gou Wen. Other names: Wu Shan (crow fan), Wu Pu (crow reed). Grows in river valleys.

She Gan (Belamcanda / blackberry lily):
Wu Pu says: She Gan — taste bitter, balanced. Primary uses: cough with counterflow qi, throat impediment (laryngitis/pharyngitis), throat pain preventing rest and breathing, disperses urgent qi, abdominal counterflow evil qi, great heat from food and drink. Another name: Wu Shan; another name: Wu Pu. Grows in river valleys.

The Mingyi says: another name is Wu Yu; another name is Wu Chui; another name is Cao Jiang. Grows in the open fields of Nanyang. The root is harvested on the third day of the third month and dried in the shade.

Ruǔ (䕡茹): Flavor salty, neutral. Governs heart pain, warms the interior, eliminates chronic white-patch skin disease (vitiligo), pinworms, snake-bite venom, abdominal masses and various worms. An alternate name is Gǔlú; grows in ponds and marshes.

The Míng Physicians say: It grows in the Eastern Sea and in Bóhǎi, Zhāngwǔ county. Harvested in the eighth month and dried in the shade.

Commentary from the Ěryǎ states: [various philological notes on variant names and textual identifications with Jūlíng or Yīnzhī; the commentator notes uncertainty about which name is correct and declines to settle the question.]

Báijí and Lì: [the Yùlǎn version reads:] Flavor bitter, neutral. Governs swellings, festering sores, injuries to the yin regions, dead muscle tissue, evil qi in the stomach, robber-wind, ghost-strike, and lax, unresponsive impediment. Alternate names: Gāngēn, Liánjícǎo. Grows in river valleys.

Wú Pǔ says: Shennong [classifies it as] bitter; the Yellow Emperor [classifies it as] acrid; Shì [the Elder] as greatly cold; Léi Gōng as acrid and non-toxic. The leaves resemble ginger; the flower of the lí lú opens upward in the tenth month in purple-red color; the root is white. Harvested in the second, eighth, and ninth months.

The Míng Physicians say: It grows in Běishān, Yuānjù, and Yuèshān.

Annotation: The text on Lord Yáng Gōng's method of taking huángjīng says huángjīng is another name for báijí; it is also an alternate name for huángjīng. Today physicians list huángjīng separately.

The Míng Physicians say: Cháng Shān — roots harvested in the twelfth month and dried in the shade.

Dàjǐ (Euphorbia): Flavor bitter, cold. Governs gu toxin, twelve kinds of edema and fullness, acute pain, accumulations and gatherings, wind striking the skin with rash-pain, and vomiting counterflow. An alternate name is Qióngjù. [Textual note: the ancient commentary suggests this entry and the following "grows in river marshes" may originally have been one entry — three characters noted by the editor.]

Commentary from the Ěryǎ: [Guo Pu notes] this is today's medicinal herb Dàjǐ, which expels water. The Huáinánzǐ, "Miùchēng" chapter, also says: Dàjǐ expels water.

Zéqī (Euphorbia helioscopia): Flavor bitter, slightly cold. Governs skin heat, distension of the abdomen, water qi, puffy swelling of the four limbs and face, and insufficiency of male yin qi. Grows in river marshes.

The Míng Physicians say: An alternate name is Qījīng; it is the seedling of Dàjǐ. Grows on Tàishān. Stems and leaves harvested on the third day of the third month and the seventh day of the seventh month, and dried in the shade.

Commentary from the Guǎngyǎ: Tàijīng is Zéqī.

Gan Sui (Euphorbia kansui): Flavor bitter, cold. Governs large-abdomen hernia-masses, abdominal fullness, facial and ocular puffiness, retained fluids and undigested food; breaks up concretions, firm accumulations, and clumps; promotes passage through the water-grain pathway. Another name: Zhutian. Grows in river valleys.

Wu Pu says: Gan Sui is also called Zhutian, Ze, Chongze, Guichou, Linggao, Gangao, and Ganze. According to Shennong and Tongjun it is bitter and toxic; according to Qibo and Leigong it is toxic and requires collection of the root in the second and eighth months, then dried in the shade.

The Mingyi says: Also named Gangao, Lingze, and Chongze; grows in Zhongshan. Root collected in the second month, dried in the shade.

Examination: The Guangya says Lingze is Gan Sui. The Fanzi Jiran says Gan Sui comes from the Sanfu region.

Bai Lian (Ampelopsis japonica): Flavor bitter, neutral. Governs abscesses, swellings, ulcers, and sores; disperses bound qi; stops pain; eliminates heat; redness of the eyes; childhood fright-epilepsy; warm malaria; swelling and pain in women's genitalia. Another name: Mianhe. Another name: Baicao. Grows in mountain valleys.

The Mingyi says: Also named Baigen, also named Kunlun. Grows on Hengshan. Root collected in the second and eighth months, dried in the sun.

Examination: The Shuowen says tu is white and yellow, sometimes written as ji. The Maoshi says ji vine. Lu Ji's commentary says ji resembles the wuluan tree; its leaves are full and fine; its seeds are jet black like swallow droppings and cannot be eaten. People of the secluded regions call it wufu; its stems and leaves are fed to cattle to eliminate heat. The Erya says lu yao biao jiang. Guo Pu says this is uncertain. According to the Pian, yao is white ji. The classic gives "Mianhe" as another name, which sounds close to this and is likely the same plant.

Qing Xiang Zi (Celosia argentea seed): Flavor bitter, slightly cold. Governs pathogenic qi; heat in the skin; wind itching and body pruritus; kills the three worms. Another name: Cao Jueming; treats cracked or discolored lips and mouth. Another name: Caohao. Another name: Qihao. Grows in flat valleys.

The Mingyi says: Grows alongside roads. Leaves collected on the third day of the third month, dried in the shade. Seeds collected in the fifth and sixth months.

Examination: The Weilüe records that during the Chupingzhong period there was an Elder of the Green Ox who regularly took Qing Xiang Zi. The character xiang in the text should be written as xiang (箱).

Master Wu Pu says: Wolf's Tooth (Langya) — also called Zhilan, also called Wolf's Teeth, also called Great Tooth, also called Baozi. According to Shennong and the Yellow Emperor: bitter, toxic. According to Tongjun: or salty. According to Qibo and Lei Gong and Bian Que: bitter. It has no [toxicity noted by some]. Grows in Wanju. Leaves green, roots red. Flowers in the sixth and seventh months, fruits in the eighth month; the fruit is black. Harvested in the first and eighth months; roots are dried in the sun.
The Mingyi records: also called Wolf's Teeth, also called Great Tooth. Grows in Huainan and Wanju. Roots collected in the eighth month, dried in the sun.

Annotation: Fan Zi's Jiran records: Wolf's Tooth comes from the Three Adjunct Regions; the white-colored specimens are the best.

Sheep's Sorrel (Yangti): flavor acrid, nature warm. Governs thieving wind lodged in the skin causing crawling pain, warm-type scabies, and malign toxins and various sores. Grows in valleys.
Master Wu Pu says: Sheep's Sorrel flowers — according to Shennong and Lei Gong: acrid, toxic. Grows in Huainan. Treats thieving wind, malign toxins, and various evil qi.
The Mingyi records: also called Yuzhi. Grows on Taihang Mountain and in Huainan. Flowers collected in the third month and dried in shade.

Guang Ya records: Sheep's Sorrel (Yangti) — its flower is beautiful and bright. The Gujin Zhu records: Sheep's Sorrel flowers are yellow; if sheep eat it they die; if sheep see it their hooves scatter — hence the name Yangti. Tao Hong[jing records]...

Phytolacca (Shanglu): flavor acrid, nature balanced. Governs water swelling, hernia pain, concretions and conglomerations; eliminates abscesses and swellings; kills ghost essences and malign entities. Also called Gegen (Kudzu Root). Also called Yehu (Night Caller). Grows in valleys.
The Mingyi records: The specimens shaped like a human form possess spiritual power. Grows in Xianyang.

Annotation: The Shuowen says Ge herb is called Danglu. In the Zhouyi, Dajun Yun calls it Gelu. Zheng Xuan says Gelu is Shanglu (Phytolacca). The character Ge is simply a borrowed form; its pronunciation is like Ge. Today in Guanzhong it is also called...

Jili (Tribulus) — in Jiangdong it is called Danglu grass; its branches and leaves correspond to each other in value. The Guang Ya records: the common Ge, Mawei Hao — this is also Shanglu. The rustic characters of the merchants use Ge as a loan character with the same pronunciation. Today in Guanzhong it is also called [the same].

Sheep's Sorrel (Yangti): flavor bitter, nature cold. Governs baldness of the head, scabies and itching; eliminates heat; treats female genital erosion. [Note: the following four characters appear without the character "Jue".] Also called Dongfang Su, also called Lian Chong Lu, also called Guimu. Grows in river marshes.
The Mingyi records: also known as Ji; grows in Chenliu.

Yinyu (Skimmia japonica): Flavor bitter, warm. Governs evil qi of the five viscera, cold and heat in the chest and abdomen, emaciation resembling malaria with episodes at fixed times, wind-damp impediment pain in all the joints. Grows in river valleys.

Wu Pu says: Yinyu — also called Wancao, also called Bigong. Slightly warm, toxic. Shaped like Mangcao but finer and softer.

The Mingyi record says: Also called Wancao, also called Bigong. Grows on Taishan. Leaves are gathered on the third day of the third month and dried in the shade.

Guanzhong (shield fern, Dryopteris crassirhizoma): Flavor bitter, slightly cold. Governs evil heat qi in the abdomen and various toxins; kills three kinds of worms. Also called Guanjie, also called Guanqu, also called Baitou. Also called Hujuan, also called Bianfu.

Wu Pu says: Guanzhong — also called Guanlai, also called Guanzhong, also called Qumu, also called Guanzhong, also called Boqin, also called Yaozao, also called Bianfu, also called Huangcan. According to Shennong.

Grows in mountain valleys.

Qibo: bitter, toxic. Tunjun and Bianque: bitter. One classic says: sweet, toxic. Huangdi: salty and sour. One classic says: bitter, non-toxic. Leaves are yellow, growing in opposite pairs; the black hairs cluster together; green in both winter and summer, never aging.

Flowers in the fourth month, fruit in the eighth month, black, clustered in rows. Roots are gathered in the third and eighth months, seeds gathered in the fifth month in Shao Shi Shan. Roots gathered in the second and eighth months and dried in the shade.

The Mingyi record says: Also called Boping, also called Yaozao. This herb is called Chitou; grows at Yuanshan and at Wanju and Shaoshi Mountain. Guo Pu says: leaves are round and pointed, stems hairy, spreading black along the ground, does not die in winter or summer. Also called Jue.

Commentary: the Shuowen says it is a kind of Mao grass. The Guangya says Guanjie is Guanzhong. Guo Pu in the Erya says Bianfu — stops diarrhea with Guanzhong. Guo Pu in the Erya also says Bianfu — this is the same plant.

Qu (another entry) further says above: Bianfu governs cold damage, warm malaria, the twelve waters, breaks up accumulations and masses, large wall-like abscesses and fistulas, flushes the intestines and stomach, removes lingering food stagnation, cold and heat evil qi, promotes water passages. Grows in river valleys.

Lianhua (Ampelopsis): Flavor bitter, balanced, cold. Governs cold damage and warm malaria.

The Mingyi record says: Grows in Xianyang and at Zhongmu in Henan. Flowers gathered in the sixth month and dried in the shade.

Yazi (wolf's tooth, Agrimonia): Flavor bitter, cold. Governs evil qi, heat qi, scabies and itching, malignant sores and wounds, scabies; expels white worms. Also called Langya. Grows in river valleys.

The Illustrious Physicians say: another name is "Nai He Cao" [Nahe Herb]. It grows on high mountains and in open fields. Collected in the fourth month.

Commentary: Tao Hongjing says that near the roots there is a white downy covering resembling the white head of a person, hence the name.

Ghost [Gui] Herb
Wu [Pu]: taste acrid, warm. Governs: killing gu-toxins, ghost-possession, spirit-creature infestations; dispels foul qi and inauspiciousness; expels evil and resolves the hundred poisons. One name: Juesi [Sparrow Rhinoceros]. One name: Mamu Dugong [Horse-Eye Poison Duke]. One name: Jiu Yue. Grows in mountain valleys.

The Illustrious Physicians say: another name Tian Yue; another name Jiu Yue; another name Tian Yue; another name Que Xi; another name Mamu Gong. One name: Jie Du [Antitoxin]. Grows in the mountain valleys of Jiuzhen and Yuanju. Collect the roots in the second and eighth months. [Imperial览]

Wu Pu says: one name Jiu Yue. Collect in the second and eighth months. [Imperial览]

Sheep Peach [Yang Tao]
The Illustrious Physicians say: one name Tian Yue; one name Jie Du. Grows in the mountain valleys of Jiuzhen and Yuanju. Collect roots in the second and eighth months.

Wu [Pu]: taste bitter, cold. Governs: sudden fever, body suddenly turning red, wind-water accumulations, malignant sores; eliminates children's fever. Collect in the second month. One name: Ghost Peach. One name: Sheep Intestine. Grows in river valleys.

Commentary: Shuowen says: "Chang Chang Chu, a type of blade-cutting plant." One name Yu Yi; one name Zhi Yi; one name Yang Tao. The Guangya says: grows in mountain forests and open fields, collected in the second month and dried in the shade. One name Ghost Peach. One name Sheep Intestine. Grows in river valleys.

Considered to be: Chu Pi; Zhang Guanya says Chang Chu is a blade-cutting plant; Lu Ji says it is now called Yang Tao [Sheep Peach], or called Ghost Peach. The leaves resemble peach leaves; the flowers are white; the seeds are like small wheat grains, reddish, resembling a peach; the Mao Shi [Book of Odes] says "In the lowlands grows Chang Chu." People today—

The Nong Chu tradition says Chang Chu is a blade-cutting plant. Lu Ji says: today's Yang Tao is this plant. The leaves are long and narrow, flowers purple-red in color; its branches and stems are slender, growing over one foot, trailing as a vine over other plants. People today—

Consider it: mud-irrigated, heavy, and not like a willow. Near the lower root, when cut with a knife, the bark and stem can be roasted in hot ash until they peel off, and can be used to wrap writing-brush tubes.

Female Verdure [Nü Qing]
Wu Pu says: Female Verdure, one name Huo. According to Shennong and Huangdi: warm; repels evil, kills gu-toxins, expels foul evil qi, dispels ghost-fever and malaria, wards off inauspiciousness. One name: Sparrow Gourd. [Imperial览, written as—]

Female Verdure: taste acrid, balanced [ping]. Governs: gu-toxins; expels evil malignant qi; kills ghost-fever and malarial disease; wards off inauspiciousness. One name: Sparrow Gourd. [Imperial览, written as—]

The Illustrious Physicians say: it is the root of She Han [Snake-Embrace herb]. Grows at Zhuyai. Collected in the eighth month, dried in the shade.

Commentary: the Guangya says Female Verdure is Wu Ge. The Erya says Cai Wan Lan is a branch. The tradition says Wan—
